## Purpose and Scope

This page provides an overview of training neural network potentials in TorchANI. Training involves optimizing the parameters of ANI models to predict molecular energies and forces from atomic coordinates. This page covers the high-level architecture, core components, and data flow involved in the training process.

For detailed information on specific aspects of training:
- See [Training Workflow](#7.1) for a complete walkthrough of the training loop implementation
- See [Data Preparation for Training](#7.2) for batching strategies and data transforms
- See [Force Training](#7.3) for force matching considerations
- See [Using Pre-built Models](#5.1) for loading pre-trained models instead of training from scratch
- See [Building Custom Models](#5.3) for creating custom model architectures to train

---

## Training Architecture Overview

The training process in TorchANI consists of several interconnected components that work together to optimize neural network potentials.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph "Data Pipeline"
        RawData["Raw Dataset<br/>(HDF5/Parquet/Zarr)"]
        ANIDataset["ANIDataset<br/>Map-style access"]
        Batcher["Batcher<br/>divide_and_batch()"]
        Transforms["Transforms<br/>SubtractSAE, etc."]
        BatchedDS["BatchedDataset<br/>(Training/Validation)"]
        DataLoader["DataLoader<br/>Iteration"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Model & Computation"
        ModelInit["Model Initialization<br/>simple_ani() or Assembler"]
        ANIModel["ANI Model<br/>Neural Networks"]
        Forward["Forward Pass<br/>model((species, coords))"]
        AEVComp["AEVComputer<br/>Feature extraction"]
        NNComp["Neural Networks<br/>Energy prediction"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Training Loop"
        Batch["Get Batch<br/>species, coords, energies"]
        EnergyLoss["Energy Loss<br/>MSE"]
        ForceLoss["Force Loss<br/>forces_for_training()"]
        TotalLoss["Total Loss<br/>Weighted sum"]
        Backward["Backward Pass<br/>loss.backward()"]
        OptStep["Optimizer Step<br/>optimizer.step()"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Validation & Management"
        ValidLoop["Validation Loop<br/>validate()"]
        RMSE["RMSE Calculation"]
        Scheduler["LR Scheduler<br/>ReduceLROnPlateau"]
        Checkpoint["Save Checkpoints<br/>torch.save()"]
    end
    
    RawData --> ANIDataset
    ANIDataset --> Batcher
    Batcher --> Transforms
    Transforms --> BatchedDS
    BatchedDS --> DataLoader
    
    ModelInit --> ANIModel
    ANIModel --> AEVComp
    AEVComp --> NNComp
    NNComp --> Forward
    
    DataLoader --> Batch
    Batch --> Forward
    Forward --> EnergyLoss
    Forward --> ForceLoss
    EnergyLoss --> TotalLoss
    ForceLoss --> TotalLoss
    TotalLoss --> Backward
    Backward --> OptStep
    OptStep --> ANIModel
    
    BatchedDS --> ValidLoop
    ANIModel --> ValidLoop
    ValidLoop --> RMSE
    RMSE --> Scheduler
    Scheduler --> ANIModel
    RMSE --> Checkpoint
    
    style ANIModel fill:#f9f9f9
    style TotalLoss fill:#f9f9f9
    style BatchedDS fill:#f9f9f9
```

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:1-212](), [torchani/datasets/batching.py:1-700](), [torchani/grad.py:1-400]()

---

## Core Training Components

### Model Initialization

Models for training can be created using either the `simple_ani()` function or the `Assembler` class. The model typically consists of:

| Component | Class/Module | Purpose |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| AEV Computer | `AEVComputer` | Computes atomic environment vectors from coordinates |
| Neural Networks | `ANINetworks` or `Ensemble` | Predicts atomic energies from AEVs |
| Self Energies | `SelfEnergy` | Adds ground-state atomic energies |
| Additional Potentials | `RepulsionXTB`, etc. | Optional repulsion/dispersion corrections |

The neural network parameters are what get optimized during training. Self energies and additional potentials typically remain fixed.

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:73-73](), [torchani/arch.py]()

### Data Pipeline

The data pipeline prepares molecular conformations for training through several stages:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Source["Data Source<br/>ANIDataset"]
    Batcher["Batcher.divide_and_batch()"]
    Train["Training Split<br/>ANIBatchedDataset"]
    Valid["Validation Split<br/>ANIBatchedDataset"]
    Transform["Transforms<br/>Applied on-the-fly"]
    TrainLoader["Training DataLoader"]
    ValidLoader["Validation DataLoader"]
    
    Source --> Batcher
    Batcher -->|"split ratio"| Train
    Batcher -->|"split ratio"| Valid
    Train --> Transform
    Valid --> Transform
    Transform --> TrainLoader
    Transform --> ValidLoader
    
    style Batcher fill:#f9f9f9
    style Transform fill:#f9f9f9
```

Key classes and methods:

- **`ANIDataset`**: Map-style dataset providing access to individual conformers
- **`Batcher`**: Splits data into training/validation and creates batches
  - `divide_and_batch()`: Main method that performs splitting and batching
- **`ANIBatchedDataset`**: Pre-batched dataset for efficient iteration
- **`ANIBatchedInMemoryDataset`**: Cached version stored in RAM
- **`Transform`**: Base class for data preprocessing operations
- **`SubtractSAE`**: Subtracts self-atomic energies from total energies

**Sources:** [torchani/datasets/batching.py:238-676](), [torchani/transforms.py:1-231](), [examples/training.py:23-53]()

### Data Transforms

Transforms preprocess the data before training. Common transforms include:

| Transform | Purpose | Applied to |
|-----------|---------|------------|
| `SubtractSAE` | Subtract self-atomic energies | Energies |
| `SubtractRepulsionXTB` | Subtract xTB repulsion | Energies, Forces |
| `SubtractTwoBodyDispersionD3` | Subtract D3 dispersion | Energies, Forces |
| `Compose` | Chain multiple transforms | All properties |

Transforms can be applied:
1. During batching (permanent, stored in batched dataset)
2. On-the-fly during iteration (via `transform` parameter)
3. Directly on batches in the training loop

**Sources:** [torchani/transforms.py:43-231](), [examples/training.py:55-69]()

### Loss Functions

Training typically involves two types of losses:

#### Energy Loss

The energy loss compares predicted molecular energies to target energies. The standard formulation uses MSE normalized by the square root of the number of atoms:

```python
energy_loss = (mse(predicted_energies, target_energies) / num_atoms.sqrt()).mean()
```

This normalization helps ensure that molecules of different sizes contribute equally to the loss.

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:172-174]()

#### Force Loss

Force loss is computed by taking gradients of predicted energies with respect to coordinates, then comparing to target forces. The `forces_for_training()` helper function computes forces with the appropriate gradient graph configuration:

```python
predicted_forces = forces_for_training(predicted_energies, coordinates)
force_loss = (mse(predicted_forces, target_forces).sum(dim=(1, 2)) / num_atoms).mean()
```

Forces are normalized by the number of atoms to maintain balanced contributions across molecules of different sizes.

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:169-177](), [torchani/grad.py:82-83]()

#### Combined Loss

The total loss combines energy and force components with a weighting coefficient:

```python
loss = energy_loss + force_coefficient * force_loss
```

The `force_coefficient` (typically 0.1) balances the relative importance of energy and force matching.

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:148-180]()

### Optimization

Training uses standard PyTorch optimizers. Common choices include:

| Optimizer | Typical Use | Key Parameters |
|-----------|-------------|----------------|
| `AdamW` | General purpose | `lr=0.5e-3`, `weight_decay=1e-6` |
| `Adam` | Alternative to AdamW | `lr=1e-3` |

Learning rate scheduling is typically handled by `ReduceLROnPlateau`, which reduces the learning rate when validation error plateaus:

```python
scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau(
    optimizer,
    factor=0.5,
    patience=100,
    threshold=0,
)
```

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:76-86]()

### Validation and Checkpointing

Validation runs after each epoch to assess model performance on held-out data. The validation process:

1. Sets model to evaluation mode (`model.train(False)`)
2. Disables gradients (`with torch.no_grad()`)
3. Computes predictions on validation batches
4. Calculates RMSE in kcal/mol units
5. Steps the learning rate scheduler
6. Saves checkpoints if performance improves

Two types of checkpoints are typically maintained:
- **Latest checkpoint**: Contains model, optimizer, and scheduler state for resuming training
- **Best model checkpoint**: Contains only the best model state by validation RMSE

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:104-145](), [examples/training.py:186-211]()

---

## Training Data Flow

This diagram shows how data flows through a single training iteration:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start["Training Iteration Start"]
    
    GetBatch["Get Batch from DataLoader<br/>batch = next(training)"]
    ToDevice["Transfer to Device<br/>batch.to(device)"]
    ExtractData["Extract Tensors<br/>species, coordinates, energies"]
    
    ZeroGrad["Zero Gradients<br/>optimizer.zero_grad()"]
    
    Forward["Forward Pass<br/>output = model((species, coords))"]
    PredEnergy["predicted_energies = output.energies"]
    
    CalcForces{"Force Training?"}
    GetForces["Compute Forces<br/>forces_for_training(energies, coords)"]
    
    EnergyLoss["Compute Energy Loss<br/>mse(...) / num_atoms.sqrt()"]
    ForceLossComp["Compute Force Loss<br/>mse(...).sum(dims) / num_atoms"]
    CombineLoss["Combine Losses<br/>energy_loss + coef * force_loss"]
    
    Backward["Backward Pass<br/>loss.backward()"]
    OptStep["Optimizer Step<br/>optimizer.step()"]
    
    NextIter["Next Iteration"]
    
    Start --> GetBatch
    GetBatch --> ToDevice
    ToDevice --> ExtractData
    ExtractData --> ZeroGrad
    ZeroGrad --> Forward
    Forward --> PredEnergy
    PredEnergy --> CalcForces
    
    CalcForces -->|"Yes"| GetForces
    CalcForces -->|"No"| EnergyLoss
    GetForces --> EnergyLoss
    
    EnergyLoss --> ForceLossComp
    ForceLossComp --> CombineLoss
    CombineLoss --> Backward
    Backward --> OptStep
    OptStep --> NextIter
    
    style Forward fill:#f9f9f9
    style CombineLoss fill:#f9f9f9
```

**Key Methods and Classes:**

| Code Entity | Location | Purpose |
|-------------|----------|---------|
| `BatchedDataset.as_dataloader()` | [torchani/datasets/batching.py:46-64]() | Creates PyTorch DataLoader |
| `model((species, coordinates))` | Model forward method | Computes energies from inputs |
| `forces_for_training()` | [torchani/grad.py:82-83]() | Computes forces with gradient graph |
| `optimizer.zero_grad()` | PyTorch | Clears accumulated gradients |
| `loss.backward()` | PyTorch | Computes parameter gradients |
| `optimizer.step()` | PyTorch | Updates model parameters |

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:156-184](), [torchani/grad.py:82-83]()

---

## Quick Start Training Example

The complete training example can be found in [examples/training.py:1-212](). Here's the structure:

### Setup Phase

```python
# Device selection
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

# Create batched datasets
batched_dataset_path = Path("./batched_dataset").resolve()
if not batched_dataset_path.exists():
    torchani.datasets.create_batched_dataset(
        ds,
        dest_path=batched_dataset_path,
        batch_size=2560,
        splits={"training": 0.8, "validation": 0.2},
    )

# Load datasets
train_ds = ANIBatchedDataset(batched_dataset_path, split="training")
valid_ds = ANIBatchedDataset(batched_dataset_path, split="validation")

# Optional: Cache in memory
train_ds = train_ds.cache()
valid_ds = valid_ds.cache()

# Create model
model = simple_ani(("H", "C", "N", "O"), lot="wb97x-631gd", repulsion=True)
model.to(device)
```

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:22-98]()

### Training Loop

```python
for epoch in range(scheduler.last_epoch, max_epochs + 1):
    for batch in training:
        batch = {k: v.to(device, non_blocking=True) for k, v in batch.items()}
        
        # Forward pass
        output = model((batch["species"], batch["coordinates"].float()))
        predicted_energies = output.energies
        
        # Compute loss
        if force_training:
            predicted_forces = forces_for_training(predicted_energies, coordinates)
            energy_loss = (mse(predicted_energies, target_energies) / num_atoms.sqrt()).mean()
            force_loss = (mse(predicted_forces, target_forces).sum(dim=(1, 2)) / num_atoms).mean()
            loss = energy_loss + force_coefficient * force_loss
        else:
            loss = (mse(predicted_energies, target_energies) / num_atoms.sqrt()).mean()
        
        # Backward pass
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
    
    # Validation and checkpointing
    rmse = validate(model, validation)
    if scheduler.is_better(rmse, scheduler.best):
        torch.save(model.state_dict(), best_model_state_checkpoint_path)
    scheduler.step(rmse)
```

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:151-211]()

---

## Batching Strategies

The `Batcher` class provides flexible data splitting and batching:

### Splits

Divide data into named splits with specified fractions:

```python
splits = {"training": 0.8, "validation": 0.2}
```

The splits are created by shuffling all conformers and dividing according to the specified fractions.

### Folds

For cross-validation or ensemble training, use folds instead of splits:

```python
folds = 5  # Creates training0/validation0, training1/validation1, etc.
```

Each fold uses a different subset as validation, enabling k-fold cross-validation.

### Batch Size and Padding

Batches are padded to accommodate molecules of different sizes. Padding values are specified in the `padding` parameter:

| Property | Default Padding | Purpose |
|----------|----------------|---------|
| `species` | -1 | Marks padded atoms |
| `coordinates` | 0.0 | Zero coordinates for padding |
| `energies` | 0.0 | Zero energy for padding |
| `forces` | 0.0 | Zero forces for padding |

**Sources:** [torchani/datasets/batching.py:238-393](), [torchani/utils.py]()

---

## Performance Considerations

### Memory Management

**In-Memory Caching:**
- Call `.cache()` on `ANIBatchedDataset` to load all batches into RAM
- Significantly faster iteration but requires substantial memory
- Automatically pins memory if CUDA is available

**Disk-Backed Datasets:**
- Use `ANIBatchedDataset` without caching for large datasets
- Supports multiprocessing via DataLoader's `num_workers`
- Slower but memory-efficient

**Sources:** [torchani/datasets/batching.py:189-211](), [examples/training.py:48-53]()

### Batch Size Selection

Typical batch sizes:
- **Small models/GPUs**: 1024-2560 conformers
- **Large models/GPUs**: 5120+ conformers
- **CPU training**: 256-1024 conformers

Larger batches provide more stable gradients but require more memory.

### Multi-GPU Training

TorchANI models are compatible with PyTorch's `DataParallel` and `DistributedDataParallel` for multi-GPU training, though specific examples are not provided in the basic training script.

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:32-32]()

# Page: Training Workflow

# Training Workflow

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [examples/training.py](examples/training.py)
- [tests/test_aev.py](tests/test_aev.py)
- [tests/test_energies.py](tests/test_energies.py)
- [tests/test_ensemble.py](tests/test_ensemble.py)
- [tests/test_forces.py](tests/test_forces.py)
- [torchani/grad.py](torchani/grad.py)

</details>



This page describes the complete training workflow for ANI neural network potentials in TorchANI. It covers the training loop structure, loss computation (energy and force matching), validation procedures, checkpointing mechanisms, and learning rate scheduling. For information about preparing datasets before training, see [Data Preparation for Training](#7.2). For specific details about force training with gradient computation, see [Force Training](#7.3).

## Overview

The training workflow in TorchANI follows standard PyTorch deep learning patterns with specialized loss functions for molecular property prediction. The process involves iterating over batched molecular conformations, computing energy and optionally force predictions, calculating losses, and updating neural network parameters via backpropagation.

Sources: [examples/training.py:1-212]()

## Training Loop Architecture

The training workflow consists of several interconnected components that execute in a specific order within each epoch:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    DataLoader["DataLoader<br/>torch.utils.data.DataLoader"]
    Batch["Batch Dictionary<br/>{species, coordinates, energies, forces}"]
    ToDevice["Transfer to Device<br/>.to(device)"]
    
    Model["ANI Model<br/>torchani.arch.ANI"]
    Forward["Forward Pass<br/>model((species, coordinates))"]
    Output["Output<br/>.energies"]
    
    EnergyLoss["Energy Loss<br/>MSELoss"]
    ForceComp["Force Computation<br/>forces_for_training()"]
    ForceLoss["Force Loss<br/>MSELoss"]
    Weighted["Weighted Sum<br/>energy_loss + force_coeff * force_loss"]
    
    ZeroGrad["optimizer.zero_grad()"]
    Backward["loss.backward()"]
    Step["optimizer.step()"]
    
    Validate["validate()<br/>Compute RMSE"]
    Scheduler["scheduler.step(rmse)"]
    Checkpoint["torch.save()<br/>State Dicts"]
    
    DataLoader --> Batch
    Batch --> ToDevice
    ToDevice --> Forward
    Model --> Forward
    Forward --> Output
    
    Output --> EnergyLoss
    Output --> ForceComp
    ForceComp --> ForceLoss
    
    EnergyLoss --> Weighted
    ForceLoss --> Weighted
    
    Weighted --> ZeroGrad
    ZeroGrad --> Backward
    Backward --> Step
    Step --> DataLoader
    
    Step --> Validate
    Validate --> Scheduler
    Validate --> Checkpoint
    Scheduler --> DataLoader
```

Sources: [examples/training.py:151-211]()

## Model Initialization

Before training begins, a model must be instantiated and configured. TorchANI provides factory functions for quick setup or custom assembly for full control:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SimpleANI["simple_ani()<br/>torchani.arch.simple_ani"]
    Config["Configuration<br/>symbols, lot, repulsion"]
    Model["ANI Model Instance<br/>torchani.arch.ANI"]
    
    LoadState["Load State Dict<br/>checkpoint['model']"]
    ToDevice["Transfer to Device<br/>.to(device, dtype)"]
    TrainMode["Set Train Mode<br/>.train(True)"]
    
    SimpleANI --> Config
    Config --> Model
    
    LoadState --> Model
    Model --> ToDevice
    ToDevice --> TrainMode
```

The typical initialization sequence involves:

1. **Create model** using `simple_ani()` or `Assembler` pattern
2. **Load checkpoint** if resuming training
3. **Transfer to device** and set appropriate dtype
4. **Enable training mode**

Sources: [examples/training.py:73-98]()

## Optimizer and Scheduler Setup

Training requires configuring an optimizer and learning rate scheduler:

| Component | Class | Key Parameters |
|-----------|-------|----------------|
| Optimizer | `torch.optim.AdamW` | `lr`, `weight_decay`, `params` |
| LR Scheduler | `torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau` | `factor`, `patience`, `threshold` |

The optimizer operates only on the neural network parameters:

```python
optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(
    params=model.neural_networks.parameters(),
    lr=0.5e-3,
    weight_decay=1e-6,
)
```

The learning rate scheduler monitors validation RMSE and reduces learning rate when progress plateaus:

```python
scheduler = torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau(
    optimizer,
    factor=0.5,
    patience=100,
    threshold=0,
)
```

Sources: [examples/training.py:76-86]()

## Data Loading for Training

The training loop consumes data through PyTorch's `DataLoader` interface. TorchANI's `BatchedDataset` provides efficient pre-batched data access:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    BatchedDS["ANIBatchedDataset<br/>split='training'"]
    Cache["Optional Cache<br/>.cache()"]
    DataLoader["as_dataloader()<br/>num_workers"]
    
    Iterator["Batch Iterator<br/>for batch in dataloader"]
    Dict["Batch Dictionary<br/>species, coordinates,<br/>energies, forces"]
    
    BatchedDS --> Cache
    Cache --> DataLoader
    DataLoader --> Iterator
    Iterator --> Dict
```

Key considerations:

- **Caching**: Call `.cache()` to load entire dataset into memory for faster iteration
- **Multiprocessing**: Set `num_workers` for parallel data loading (use 0 when cached)
- **Pin Memory**: Automatically handled by `ANIBatchedDataset` when cached

Sources: [examples/training.py:36-53]()

## Forward Pass and Loss Computation

Each training iteration performs a forward pass through the model and computes losses:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Batch["Batch from DataLoader"]
    Transfer["Transfer to Device<br/>batch.to(device)"]
    
    Species["Extract species<br/>batch['species']"]
    Coords["Extract coordinates<br/>batch['coordinates'].float()"]
    TargetE["Extract target energies<br/>batch['energies'].float()"]
    TargetF["Extract target forces<br/>batch['forces'].float()"]
    
    NumAtoms["Compute num_atoms<br/>(species >= 0).sum()"]
    
    Forward["Model Forward<br/>model((species, coordinates))"]
    PredE["Predicted Energies<br/>output.energies"]
    
    PredF["Compute Forces<br/>forces_for_training(energies, coords)"]
    
    ELoss["Energy Loss<br/>MSE / sqrt(num_atoms)"]
    FLoss["Force Loss<br/>MSE.sum(1,2) / num_atoms"]
    
    TotalLoss["Total Loss<br/>energy_loss + coeff * force_loss"]
    
    Batch --> Transfer
    Transfer --> Species
    Transfer --> Coords
    Transfer --> TargetE
    Transfer --> TargetF
    
    Species --> NumAtoms
    Species --> Forward
    Coords --> Forward
    Coords --> PredF
    
    Forward --> PredE
    PredE --> PredF
    PredE --> ELoss
    PredF --> FLoss
    
    TargetE --> ELoss
    TargetF --> FLoss
    NumAtoms --> ELoss
    NumAtoms --> FLoss
    
    ELoss --> TotalLoss
    FLoss --> TotalLoss
```

### Energy-Only Loss

For energy-only training (common in early training phases):

```python
num_atoms = (species >= 0).sum(dim=1, dtype=target_energies.dtype)
loss = (mse(predicted_energies, target_energies) / num_atoms.sqrt()).mean()
```

The division by `sqrt(num_atoms)` normalizes the loss across molecules of different sizes.

### Combined Energy and Force Loss

When `force_training=True`:

```python
predicted_forces = forces_for_training(predicted_energies, coordinates)
energy_loss = (mse(predicted_energies, target_energies) / num_atoms.sqrt()).mean()
force_loss = (mse(predicted_forces, target_forces).sum(dim=(1, 2)) / num_atoms).mean()
loss = energy_loss + force_coefficient * force_loss
```

The `forces_for_training()` function computes forces via automatic differentiation with `retain_graph=True` and `create_graph=True` to enable backpropagation through the force computation.

Sources: [examples/training.py:148-180](), [torchani/grad.py:82-83]()

## Backward Pass and Optimization

After loss computation, the backward pass and parameter update follow standard PyTorch patterns:

| Step | Operation | Purpose |
|------|-----------|---------|
| 1 | `optimizer.zero_grad()` | Clear previous gradients |
| 2 | `loss.backward()` | Compute gradients via backpropagation |
| 3 | `optimizer.step()` | Update model parameters |

```python
optimizer.zero_grad()
loss.backward()
optimizer.step()
```

This sequence is repeated for each batch in the training dataset.

Sources: [examples/training.py:182-184]()

## Validation

At the end of each epoch, validation is performed to monitor training progress and guide learning rate scheduling:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    SetEval["model.train(False)"]
    NoGrad["with torch.no_grad()"]
    
    Loop["for batch in validation"]
    ToDevice["batch.to(device)"]
    Forward["model((species, coords))"]
    
    SE["Accumulate Squared Error<br/>(pred - target)^2.sum()"]
    Count["Accumulate Count<br/>batch size"]
    
    RMSE["Compute RMSE<br/>sqrt(SE / count)"]
    Convert["Convert to kcal/mol<br/>hartree2kcalpermol()"]
    
    SetTrain["model.train(True)"]
    Return["Return RMSE"]
    
    SetEval --> NoGrad
    NoGrad --> Loop
    Loop --> ToDevice
    ToDevice --> Forward
    Forward --> SE
    Forward --> Count
    
    SE --> RMSE
    Count --> RMSE
    RMSE --> Convert
    Convert --> SetTrain
    SetTrain --> Return
```

The validation function computes RMSE across the entire validation set:

```python
def validate(model: ANI, validation: torch.utils.data.DataLoader) -> float:
    squared_error = 0.0
    count = 0
    model.train(False)
    with torch.no_grad():
        for properties in validation:
            properties = {k: v.to(device, non_blocking=True) for k, v in properties.items()}
            species = properties["species"]
            coordinates = properties["coordinates"].float()
            target_energies = properties["energies"].float()
            output = model((species, coordinates))
            predicted_energies = output.energies
            squared_error += (predicted_energies - target_energies).pow(2).sum().item()
            count += predicted_energies.shape[0]
    model.train(True)
    rmse = math.sqrt(squared_error / count)
    return hartree2kcalpermol(rmse)
```

Key aspects:
- **Evaluation mode**: `model.train(False)` disables dropout and batch normalization training behavior
- **No gradients**: `torch.no_grad()` reduces memory usage and speeds computation
- **RMSE metric**: Root mean squared error provides interpretable error magnitude
- **Unit conversion**: Convert from Hartree to kcal/mol for interpretability

Sources: [examples/training.py:104-122]()

## Checkpointing and State Management

TorchANI training workflows maintain two types of checkpoints:

| Checkpoint | File | Contents | When Saved |
|------------|------|----------|------------|
| Training State | `latest_training_state.pt` | Model, optimizer, scheduler state dicts | Every epoch |
| Best Model | `best_model_state.pt` | Model state dict only | When validation RMSE improves |

### Training State Checkpoint

Saves complete training state for resumption:

```python
torch.save(
    {
        "model": model.state_dict(),
        "optimizer": optimizer.state_dict(),
        "scheduler": scheduler.state_dict(),
    },
    latest_training_state_checkpoint_path,
)
```

### Best Model Checkpoint

Saves only the model when validation improves:

```python
if scheduler.is_better(rmse, scheduler.best):
    torch.save(model.state_dict(), best_model_state_checkpoint_path)
```

### Checkpoint Loading

At training start, load existing checkpoint if available:

```python
if latest_training_state_checkpoint_path.exists():
    checkpoint = torch.load(latest_training_state_checkpoint_path, weights_only=True)
    model.load_state_dict(checkpoint["model"])
    scheduler.load_state_dict(checkpoint["scheduler"])
    optimizer.load_state_dict(checkpoint["optimizer"])
```

Sources: [examples/training.py:88-96](), [examples/training.py:138-205]()

## Learning Rate Scheduling

The `ReduceLROnPlateau` scheduler adjusts learning rate based on validation performance:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    ValidRMSE["Validation RMSE"]
    SchedulerStep["scheduler.step(rmse)"]
    
    Compare["Compare to<br/>scheduler.best"]
    
    Improve["RMSE Improved"]
    NoImprove["No Improvement<br/>for patience epochs"]
    
    UpdateBest["Update best"]
    Continue["Continue training"]
    ReduceLR["Reduce LR<br/>lr *= factor"]
    
    ValidRMSE --> SchedulerStep
    SchedulerStep --> Compare
    
    Compare --> Improve
    Compare --> NoImprove
    
    Improve --> UpdateBest
    NoImprove --> ReduceLR
    ReduceLR --> Continue
    UpdateBest --> Continue
```

Key parameters:
- **factor**: Learning rate multiplier when reducing (e.g., 0.5 halves the LR)
- **patience**: Number of epochs without improvement before reducing
- **threshold**: Minimum improvement to be considered progress

The scheduler tracks the best validation RMSE and reduces learning rate when the metric plateaus:

```python
scheduler.step(rmse)
```

Training terminates when learning rate falls below a minimum threshold:

```python
if optimizer.param_groups[0]["lr"] < min_learning_rate:
    break
```

Sources: [examples/training.py:81-86](), [examples/training.py:152-154](), [examples/training.py:195]()

## Complete Training Loop Structure

The complete epoch loop integrates all components:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start["Start Epoch"]
    CheckLR["Check LR >= min_lr"]
    
    BatchLoop["for batch in training"]
    LoadBatch["Load and transfer batch"]
    Forward["Forward pass"]
    ComputeLoss["Compute loss"]
    Backward["Backward pass"]
    OptStep["Optimizer step"]
    
    ValidStep["Validate on validation set"]
    CheckImprove["RMSE improved?"]
    
    SaveBest["Save best_model_state.pt"]
    SchedulerStep["scheduler.step(rmse)"]
    SaveState["Save latest_training_state.pt"]
    LogMetrics["Log to tensorboard"]
    
    NextEpoch["Next Epoch"]
    StopTrain["Stop Training"]
    
    Start --> CheckLR
    CheckLR -->|Yes| BatchLoop
    CheckLR -->|No| StopTrain
    
    BatchLoop --> LoadBatch
    LoadBatch --> Forward
    Forward --> ComputeLoss
    ComputeLoss --> Backward
    Backward --> OptStep
    OptStep --> BatchLoop
    
    BatchLoop --> ValidStep
    ValidStep --> CheckImprove
    
    CheckImprove -->|Yes| SaveBest
    CheckImprove -->|No| SchedulerStep
    SaveBest --> SchedulerStep
    
    SchedulerStep --> SaveState
    SaveState --> LogMetrics
    LogMetrics --> NextEpoch
    NextEpoch --> Start
```

This structure ensures:
- Proper gradient computation and parameter updates
- Regular validation and checkpointing
- Adaptive learning rate adjustment
- Training termination when learning stagnates

Sources: [examples/training.py:151-211]()

## Training Metrics and Logging

TensorBoard integration enables monitoring of training progress:

```python
tensorboard = torch.utils.tensorboard.SummaryWriter()
tensorboard.add_scalar("validation_rmse_kcalpermol", rmse, epoch)
tensorboard.add_scalar("best_validation_rmse_kcalpermol", scheduler.best, epoch)
tensorboard.add_scalar("learning_rate", optimizer.param_groups[0]["lr"], epoch)
tensorboard.add_scalar("epoch_loss_square_ha", loss, epoch)
```

Tracked metrics include:
- Current validation RMSE
- Best validation RMSE achieved
- Current learning rate
- Last batch loss value

Sources: [examples/training.py:127](), [examples/training.py:207-211]()

# Page: Data Preparation for Training

# Data Preparation for Training

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [tests/test_datasets.py](tests/test_datasets.py)
- [tests/test_datasets_batching.py](tests/test_datasets_batching.py)
- [tests/test_legacy_data.py](tests/test_legacy_data.py)
- [tests/test_sae.py](tests/test_sae.py)
- [torchani/datasets/__init__.py](torchani/datasets/__init__.py)
- [torchani/datasets/batching.py](torchani/datasets/batching.py)
- [torchani/legacy_data/__init__.py](torchani/legacy_data/__init__.py)
- [torchani/legacy_data/_pyanitools.py](torchani/legacy_data/_pyanitools.py)
- [torchani/sae.py](torchani/sae.py)
- [torchani/transforms.py](torchani/transforms.py)

</details>



This page describes how to prepare molecular datasets for training neural network potentials in TorchANI. It covers batching strategies, train/validation splitting, applying transforms to normalize data, and memory management options.

**Scope**: This page focuses on the data preparation steps that occur *after* loading raw datasets and *before* entering the training loop. For information about loading built-in datasets, see [Built-in Datasets](#6.1). For the complete training workflow including loss computation and optimization, see [Training Workflow](#7.1).

---

## Overview

Data preparation for training involves three main steps:

1. **Splitting**: Divide conformers into training and validation sets (or k-folds for cross-validation)
2. **Batching**: Group conformers into batches with padding to handle variable molecule sizes
3. **Transforming**: Apply preprocessing operations like subtracting self-atomic energies

The `Batcher` class orchestrates these steps and can save results to disk or keep them in RAM depending on dataset size and available memory.

**Workflow Diagram: From Raw Dataset to Training-Ready Batches**

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    RawData["ANIDataset\n(raw HDF5/Parquet/Zarr)"]
    Batcher["Batcher.divide_and_batch()"]
    Transform["Transform Pipeline\n(SubtractSAE, etc.)"]
    
    subgraph "Split Options"
        Splits["splits={'training': 0.8, 'validation': 0.2}"]
        Folds["folds=5\n(for cross-validation)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Storage Options"
        Disk["ANIBatchedDataset\n(disk-backed)"]
        RAM["ANIBatchedInMemoryDataset\n(RAM-cached)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output"
        TrainLoader["Training DataLoader"]
        ValidLoader["Validation DataLoader"]
    end
    
    RawData --> Batcher
    Splits --> Batcher
    Folds --> Batcher
    Transform --> Batcher
    
    Batcher --> Disk
    Batcher --> RAM
    
    Disk --> TrainLoader
    Disk --> ValidLoader
    RAM --> TrainLoader
    RAM --> ValidLoader
```

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:238-393]()

---

## The Batcher Class

The `Batcher` class is the primary interface for preparing datasets. It handles shuffling, splitting, batching, padding, and optional transformation of conformers.

### Basic Usage

```python
from torchani.datasets import Batcher, ANIDataset

# Load raw dataset
dataset = ANIDataset('/path/to/dataset.h5')

# Create batcher
batcher = Batcher(
    dest_root='default',  # or Path to custom directory
    max_batches_per_packet=200,  # memory vs speed tradeoff
    verbose=True
)

# Prepare batched datasets
batched_datasets = batcher.divide_and_batch(
    src=dataset,
    dest_dir='my_batched_dataset',
    splits={'training': 0.8, 'validation': 0.2},
    batch_size=2560,
    divs_seed=12345,  # for reproducibility
    batch_seed=67890
)

train = batched_datasets['training']
valid = batched_datasets['validation']
```

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:238-266](), [torchani/datasets/batching.py:267-393]()

### Key Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Default | Description |
|-----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `dest_root` | `Path` or `'default'` or `'ram'` | `'default'` | Where to save batched data. `'default'` uses `datasets_dir()`, `'ram'` keeps in memory |
| `max_batches_per_packet` | `int` | `200` | Number of batches to process at once. Higher = faster but more RAM |
| `verbose` | `bool` | `False` | Print progress information |

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:238-262]()

### The divide_and_batch Method

**Method Signature and Core Arguments**

```mermaid
graph TB
    Method["divide_and_batch()"]
    
    subgraph "Input"
        Src["src: ANIDataset or path(s)"]
        DestDir["dest_dir: str\n(subdirectory name)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Splitting"
        Splits["splits: Dict[str, float]\n{'training': 0.8, 'validation': 0.2}"]
        Folds["folds: int\n(e.g., 5 for 5-fold CV)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Batching"
        BatchSize["batch_size: int\n(default: 2560)"]
        Padding["padding: Dict[str, float]\nPADDING constant"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Preprocessing"
        Transform["transform: Transform\n(e.g., SubtractSAE)"]
        Properties["properties: Sequence[str]\n('energies', 'forces', etc.)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Randomization"
        DivsSeed["divs_seed: Optional[int]\n(shuffle divisions)"]
        BatchSeed["batch_seed: Optional[int]\n(shuffle batches)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output"
        Result["Dict[str, BatchedDataset]\n{'training': ..., 'validation': ...}"]
    end
    
    Src --> Method
    DestDir --> Method
    Splits --> Method
    Folds --> Method
    BatchSize --> Method
    Padding --> Method
    Transform --> Method
    Properties --> Method
    DivsSeed --> Method
    BatchSeed --> Method
    
    Method --> Result
```

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:267-393]()

### Important Parameters

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `splits` | `Optional[Dict[str, float]]` | Division fractions (must sum to 1.0). Example: `{'training': 0.8, 'validation': 0.2}` |
| `folds` | `Optional[int]` | Number of folds for cross-validation. Creates `training0`, `validation0`, `training1`, etc. |
| `batch_size` | `int` | Number of conformers per batch (default: 2560) |
| `padding` | `Optional[Dict[str, float]]` | Custom padding values. Default uses `PADDING` constant |
| `transform` | `Transform` | Transform to apply during batching (default: `identity`) |
| `properties` | `Iterable[str]` | Which properties to include. Empty means all tensor properties |
| `divs_seed` | `Optional[int]` | Random seed for division shuffling (for reproducibility) |
| `batch_seed` | `Optional[int]` | Random seed for batch shuffling (for reproducibility) |

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:267-320]()

---

## Train/Validation Splits

### Standard Split

The most common approach divides data into training and validation sets:

```python
batched_datasets = batcher.divide_and_batch(
    src=dataset,
    splits={'training': 0.8, 'validation': 0.2},
    batch_size=2560,
    divs_seed=42  # ensures reproducible splits
)

train = batched_datasets['training']
valid = batched_datasets['validation']
```

The `divs_seed` parameter controls the random shuffling before splitting. Setting it ensures the same conformers end up in training vs validation across runs.

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:343-346](), [torchani/datasets/batching.py:395-425]()

### K-Fold Cross-Validation

For ensemble training or hyperparameter tuning, use k-fold cross-validation:

```python
batched_datasets = batcher.divide_and_batch(
    src=dataset,
    folds=5,  # creates 5 training/validation pairs
    batch_size=2560,
    divs_seed=42
)

# Iterate over folds
for i in range(5):
    train = batched_datasets[f'training{i}']
    valid = batched_datasets[f'validation{i}']
    # Train model on fold i
```

This creates 10 datasets total: `training0`, `validation0`, `training1`, `validation1`, etc. Each validation set is disjoint from its corresponding training set and from all other validation sets.

**K-Fold Division Strategy**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "All Conformers (shuffled)"
        Block0["Block 0"]
        Block1["Block 1"]
        Block2["Block 2"]
        Block3["Block 3"]
        Block4["Block 4"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Fold 0"
        Train0["training0:\nBlocks 1,2,3,4"]
        Valid0["validation0:\nBlock 0"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Fold 1"
        Train1["training1:\nBlocks 0,2,3,4"]
        Valid1["validation1:\nBlock 1"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Fold 2"
        Train2["training2:\nBlocks 0,1,3,4"]
        Valid2["validation2:\nBlock 2"]
    end
    
    Block0 --> Valid0
    Block1 --> Train0
    Block2 --> Train0
    Block3 --> Train0
    Block4 --> Train0
    
    Block0 --> Train1
    Block1 --> Valid1
    Block2 --> Train1
    
    Block0 --> Train2
    Block1 --> Train2
    Block2 --> Valid2
```

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:427-452]()

---

## Applying Transforms

Transforms preprocess data during batching. The most common is subtracting self-atomic energies (SAE), which shifts the energy zero-point to improve training stability.

### Available Transforms

| Transform | Purpose | Common Use |
|-----------|---------|------------|
| `SubtractSAE` | Subtract constant atomic energies | Always recommended for training |
| `SubtractRepulsionXTB` | Subtract xTB repulsion energy | When training on top of repulsion baseline |
| `SubtractTwoBodyDispersionD3` | Subtract DFT-D3 dispersion | When training on top of dispersion baseline |
| `AtomicNumbersToIndices` | Convert atomic numbers to indices | Legacy compatibility (usually not needed) |
| `Compose` | Chain multiple transforms | Combine SAE + repulsion + dispersion |

Sources: [torchani/transforms.py:43-231]()

### Using SubtractSAE

```python
from torchani.transforms import SubtractSAE

# Define self-atomic energies for H, C, N, O (in Hartree)
sae_transform = SubtractSAE(
    symbols=('H', 'C', 'N', 'O'),
    self_energies=[-0.5, -37.8, -54.6, -75.1]
)

batched_datasets = batcher.divide_and_batch(
    src=dataset,
    splits={'training': 0.8, 'validation': 0.2},
    batch_size=2560,
    transform=sae_transform  # Applied during batching
)
```

**Note**: When using `SubtractSAE` during batching, the same transform is automatically applied when loading batches, so energies are already shifted.

Sources: [torchani/transforms.py:154-169](), [tests/test_datasets.py:144-149]()

### Composing Multiple Transforms

For complex preprocessing, chain transforms together:

```python
from torchani.transforms import (
    Compose,
    SubtractSAE,
    SubtractRepulsionXTB,
    SubtractTwoBodyDispersionD3
)

symbols = ('H', 'C', 'N', 'O')

transform_pipeline = Compose([
    SubtractSAE(symbols, [-0.5, -37.8, -54.6, -75.1]),
    SubtractRepulsionXTB(symbols=symbols),
    SubtractTwoBodyDispersionD3(symbols=symbols, functional='wB97X')
])

batched_datasets = batcher.divide_and_batch(
    src=dataset,
    splits={'training': 0.8, 'validation': 0.2},
    transform=transform_pipeline,
    batch_size=2560
)
```

Sources: [torchani/transforms.py:194-223](), [torchani/transforms.py:109-129](), [torchani/transforms.py:131-152]()

### Transform Application Timing

**Transform Pipeline During Batching**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Batching Process"
        Fetch["Fetch Conformers\nfrom Dataset"]
        Pad["Apply Padding"]
        TransformBatch["Apply Transform"]
        Save["Save Batch"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Loading Process"
        Load["Load Batch\nfrom Disk"]
        TransformLoad["Apply Transform\n(if not applied during batch)"]
        Return["Return to DataLoader"]
    end
    
    Fetch --> Pad
    Pad --> TransformBatch
    TransformBatch --> Save
    
    Save -.->|if disk-backed| Load
    Load --> TransformLoad
    TransformLoad --> Return
```

Transforms can be applied either:
1. **During batching** (more common): Transform is baked into saved batches
2. **During loading**: Transform applied on-the-fly when iterating batches

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:549-565](), [torchani/datasets/batching.py:222-225]()

---

## Memory Management Strategies

TorchANI provides three storage strategies for batched datasets, each with different memory/speed tradeoffs.

### Disk-Backed Storage (ANIBatchedDataset)

**Default for large datasets.** Batches are saved as HDF5 files and loaded on-demand.

```python
batcher = Batcher(dest_root='/path/to/storage')

batched_datasets = batcher.divide_and_batch(
    src=dataset,
    dest_dir='my_dataset',
    splits={'training': 0.8, 'validation': 0.2},
    batch_size=2560
)

# Returns ANIBatchedDataset instances
train = batched_datasets['training']  # Loads from disk on iteration
```

**Advantages:**
- Minimal memory footprint
- Can handle arbitrarily large datasets
- Batches stored at `{dest_root}/{dest_dir}/{split}/NNNNN_batch.h5`

**Disadvantages:**
- Slower iteration due to disk I/O
- Requires disk space

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:144-229](), [torchani/datasets/batching.py:567-570]()

### RAM-Cached Storage (ANIBatchedInMemoryDataset)

**Recommended for datasets that fit in memory.** All batches loaded into RAM for fast iteration.

```python
# Option 1: Cache after disk-backed creation
train_cached = train.cache(verbose=True, pin_memory=True)

# Option 2: Create directly in RAM
batcher = Batcher.in_ram(verbose=True)
batched_datasets = batcher.divide_and_batch(
    src=dataset,
    splits={'training': 0.8, 'validation': 0.2},
    batch_size=2560
)
# Returns ANIBatchedInMemoryDataset instances
```

**Advantages:**
- Fast iteration (no disk I/O)
- Can pin memory for faster GPU transfer

**Disadvantages:**
- Requires significant RAM
- Initial caching can be slow

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:83-139](), [torchani/datasets/batching.py:189-211]()

### Convenience Function: batch_all_in_ram

For small datasets, skip disk entirely:

```python
from torchani.datasets import batch_all_in_ram

# Creates single in-memory training dataset
train = batch_all_in_ram(
    src='/path/to/dataset.h5',
    batch_size=2560,
    transform=sae_transform,
    divs_seed=42,
    batch_seed=123
)
```

This function uses `splits={'training': 1.0}` internally and returns only the training set.

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:678-699]()

### Memory Management Decision Tree

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start{Dataset Size}
    
    FitsRAM{Fits in RAM?\n~tens of GB}
    SmallDataset{Very Small?\n~few GB}
    
    DiskFirst["Use Batcher with\ndest_root=Path"]
    CacheLater["Call .cache()\non datasets"]
    
    DirectRAM["Use Batcher.in_ram()"]
    
    BatchAllRAM["Use batch_all_in_ram()\nfor quick prototyping"]
    
    DiskOnly["Use disk-backed\nANIBatchedDataset"]
    
    Start -->|Large| DiskOnly
    Start -->|Medium| FitsRAM
    Start -->|Small| SmallDataset
    
    FitsRAM -->|Yes| DiskFirst
    DiskFirst --> CacheLater
    
    SmallDataset -->|Need splits| DirectRAM
    SmallDataset -->|Single training set| BatchAllRAM
```

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:238-266](), [torchani/datasets/batching.py:678-699]()

---

## Batch Padding

TorchANI batches conformers with different numbers of atoms by padding smaller molecules with dummy atoms. The `PADDING` constant defines default padding values:

```python
PADDING = {
    'species': -1,        # Padding atoms have species = -1
    'coordinates': 0.0,   # Padded coordinates are zeros
    'forces': 0.0,        # Padded forces are zeros
    'energies': 0.0       # Unused (energies are scalar per molecule)
}
```

Padding is automatically applied during batching and removed where possible to minimize memory.

Sources: [torchani/utils.py]() (PADDING constant), [torchani/datasets/batching.py:532-534](), [torchani/datasets/batching.py:553]()

### Custom Padding

Override defaults if needed:

```python
custom_padding = {
    'species': -1,
    'coordinates': 0.0,
    'forces': 0.0,
    'charges': 0,  # Add custom property padding
}

batched_datasets = batcher.divide_and_batch(
    src=dataset,
    splits={'training': 0.8, 'validation': 0.2},
    padding=custom_padding,
    batch_size=2560
)
```

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:282]()

---

## Using Batched Datasets

Once created, batched datasets integrate with PyTorch's `DataLoader`:

```python
train_loader = train.as_dataloader(
    num_workers=4,
    pin_memory=True,
    prefetch_factor=2,
    shuffle=True
)

for batch in train_loader:
    species = batch['species']       # (batch_size, max_atoms)
    coordinates = batch['coordinates'] # (batch_size, max_atoms, 3)
    energies = batch['energies']     # (batch_size,)
    
    # Training code here
```

**DataLoader Integration**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "BatchedDataset"
        Storage["Disk or RAM Storage"]
        GetItem["__getitem__(idx)"]
        Transform["Optional Transform"]
    end
    
    subgraph "DataLoader"
        Workers["Worker Processes\n(num_workers)"]
        Prefetch["Prefetch Queue\n(prefetch_factor)"]
        Shuffle["Shuffle Batches\n(shuffle=True)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Training Loop"
        Iterate["for batch in loader:"]
        Forward["model(batch)"]
    end
    
    Storage --> GetItem
    GetItem --> Transform
    Transform --> Workers
    Workers --> Prefetch
    Prefetch --> Shuffle
    Shuffle --> Iterate
    Iterate --> Forward
```

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:46-64](), [torchani/datasets/batching.py:111-130]()

### Important DataLoader Parameters

| Parameter | Recommended | Notes |
|-----------|-------------|-------|
| `num_workers` | `0` for in-memory, `4+` for disk | In-memory datasets don't support multiprocessing |
| `pin_memory` | `True` if using GPU | Faster CPU→GPU transfer |
| `prefetch_factor` | `2` | Only used if `num_workers > 0` |
| `shuffle` | `True` for training | Batches are already internally shuffled |
| `batch_size` | `None` | Must be `None` (batches are pre-formed) |

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:46-64](), [torchani/datasets/batching.py:111-130]()

---

## Complete Example: Preparing ANI-1x for Training

```python
from torchani.datasets import Batcher, ANI1x
from torchani.transforms import SubtractSAE
from torchani.sae import SelfEnergy

# 1. Load built-in dataset
dataset = ANI1x()

# 2. Create transform with GSAES
sae_transform = SelfEnergy.with_gsaes(
    symbols=('H', 'C', 'N', 'O'),
    functional='wB97X',
    basis_set='631Gd'
)
transform = SubtractSAE(
    symbols=('H', 'C', 'N', 'O'),
    self_energies=sae_transform.self_energies.tolist()
)

# 3. Create batcher
batcher = Batcher(
    dest_root='./training_data',
    max_batches_per_packet=200,
    verbose=True
)

# 4. Divide and batch
batched_datasets = batcher.divide_and_batch(
    src=dataset,
    dest_dir='ani1x_batched',
    splits={'training': 0.8, 'validation': 0.2},
    batch_size=2560,
    transform=transform,
    properties=('species', 'coordinates', 'energies', 'forces'),
    divs_seed=42,
    batch_seed=123
)

# 5. Cache for fast iteration (if enough RAM)
train = batched_datasets['training'].cache(pin_memory=True)
valid = batched_datasets['validation'].cache(pin_memory=True)

# 6. Create data loaders
train_loader = train.as_dataloader(shuffle=True)
valid_loader = valid.as_dataloader(shuffle=False)

# 7. Ready for training
for batch in train_loader:
    # Training code here
    pass
```

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:238-393](), [torchani/transforms.py:154-169](), [torchani/sae.py:48-50]()

---

## Legacy API: create_batched_dataset

For backward compatibility, TorchANI provides `create_batched_dataset`, a functional wrapper around `Batcher`:

```python
from torchani.datasets import create_batched_dataset

batched_datasets = create_batched_dataset(
    src='/path/to/dataset.h5',
    dest_path='/path/to/output',
    splits={'training': 0.8, 'validation': 0.2},
    batch_size=2560,
    transform=sae_transform,
    divs_seed=42,
    batch_seed=123,
    direct_cache=False,  # If True, creates in-memory datasets
    max_batches_per_packet=200,
    verbose=True
)
```

**Note**: New code should prefer the `Batcher` class for better clarity and control.

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:620-675]()

---

## Best Practices

1. **Always set random seeds** (`divs_seed`, `batch_seed`) for reproducible experiments
2. **Use SubtractSAE** to improve training stability and convergence
3. **Choose batch size** based on GPU memory: 1024-2560 typical for modern GPUs
4. **Cache in RAM** if dataset fits in memory for 10-100x faster iteration
5. **Use disk-backed** for large datasets to avoid memory issues
6. **Include 'forces'** in properties if training with force matching
7. **Verify splits** by checking `len(train)` and `len(valid)` after creation
8. **Monitor memory** usage during batching with `verbose=True`

Sources: [torchani/datasets/batching.py:267-393](), [torchani/transforms.py:154-169]()

---

# Page: Force Training

# Force Training

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [examples/training.py](examples/training.py)
- [tests/test_aev.py](tests/test_aev.py)
- [tests/test_energies.py](tests/test_energies.py)
- [tests/test_ensemble.py](tests/test_ensemble.py)
- [tests/test_forces.py](tests/test_forces.py)
- [torchani/grad.py](torchani/grad.py)

</details>



Force training refers to the practice of training neural network potentials using both energy and force data as training targets. This approach leverages the fact that atomic forces are the negative gradients of potential energy with respect to atomic positions, enabling models to learn from both scalar energies and vector forces simultaneously. This page covers the special considerations required for implementing force training in TorchANI.

For information about the overall training workflow, see [Training Workflow](#7.1). For data preparation including force data handling, see [Data Preparation for Training](#7.2).

## Background: Forces as Energy Gradients

In molecular systems, the force on each atom is the negative gradient of the total potential energy with respect to that atom's coordinates:

```
F = -∇E = -∂E/∂r
```

This relationship means that if we have a differentiable energy function (our neural network potential), we can compute forces through automatic differentiation. Conversely, when training with force data, we must enable gradient computation through the force calculation itself, requiring double backpropagation.

**Sources:** [torchani/grad.py:42-64]()

## Force Computation Architecture

The following diagram shows how forces are computed from energies using PyTorch's autograd system:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input["Input: species, coordinates"]
    CoordGrad["coordinates.requires_grad = True"]
    Model["model((species, coordinates))"]
    Energy["energies: Tensor"]
    AutogradGrad["torch.autograd.grad(energies.sum(), coordinates)"]
    Gradients["gradients: ∂E/∂coords"]
    Forces["forces = -gradients"]
    
    Input --> CoordGrad
    CoordGrad --> Model
    Model --> Energy
    Energy --> AutogradGrad
    CoordGrad --> AutogradGrad
    AutogradGrad --> Gradients
    Gradients --> Forces
    
    style Energy fill:#f9f9f9
    style Forces fill:#f9f9f9
```

**Sources:** [torchani/grad.py:42-64]()

## The `forces_for_training` Function

TorchANI provides a specialized function for computing forces during training that enables gradient computation through the force calculation:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Standard Force Computation"
        E1["energies"]
        C1["coordinates"]
        F1["forces(energies, coordinates)"]
        R1["retain_graph=False<br/>create_graph=False"]
        
        E1 --> F1
        C1 --> F1
        R1 -.-> F1
        F1 --> Out1["forces<br/>(no gradients)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Force Training Computation"
        E2["energies"]
        C2["coordinates"]
        F2["forces_for_training(energies, coordinates)"]
        R2["retain_graph=True<br/>create_graph=True"]
        
        E2 --> F2
        C2 --> F2
        R2 -.-> F2
        F2 --> Out2["forces<br/>(with gradients)"]
    end
```

The `forces_for_training` function is a convenience wrapper that sets the appropriate autograd flags:

| Function | `retain_graph` | `create_graph` | Use Case |
|----------|----------------|----------------|----------|
| `forces()` | `False` | `False` | Inference, validation |
| `forces_for_training()` | `True` | `True` | Training with force loss |

**Key Implementation:**
- [torchani/grad.py:82-83]() defines `forces_for_training`
- [torchani/grad.py:42-64]() defines the underlying `forces` function
- The `create_graph=True` flag enables gradient computation through forces
- The `retain_graph=True` flag preserves the computation graph for subsequent loss backpropagation

**Sources:** [torchani/grad.py:82-83](), [torchani/grad.py:42-64]()

## Implementing Force Training

The following diagram shows the complete data flow for force training:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Batch["Training Batch"]
    Species["species"]
    Coords["coordinates<br/>(requires_grad=True)"]
    TargetE["target_energies"]
    TargetF["target_forces"]
    
    Batch --> Species
    Batch --> Coords
    Batch --> TargetE
    Batch --> TargetF
    
    Model["model((species, coordinates))"]
    Species --> Model
    Coords --> Model
    
    PredE["predicted_energies"]
    Model --> PredE
    
    ForceFn["forces_for_training(predicted_energies, coordinates)"]
    PredE --> ForceFn
    Coords --> ForceFn
    PredF["predicted_forces"]
    ForceFn --> PredF
    
    ELoss["energy_loss = MSE(predicted_energies, target_energies)"]
    PredE --> ELoss
    TargetE --> ELoss
    
    FLoss["force_loss = MSE(predicted_forces, target_forces)"]
    PredF --> FLoss
    TargetF --> FLoss
    
    TotalLoss["total_loss = energy_loss + coefficient * force_loss"]
    ELoss --> TotalLoss
    FLoss --> TotalLoss
    
    Backward["loss.backward()"]
    TotalLoss --> Backward
    
    Update["optimizer.step()"]
    Backward --> Update
```

**Example Implementation from Training Script:**

The training example demonstrates force training at [examples/training.py:149-184]():

```python
# Enable force training
force_training = True
force_coefficient = 0.1

# Training loop
for batch in training:
    species = batch["species"]
    coordinates = batch["coordinates"].float()
    target_energies = batch["energies"].float()
    
    # Forward pass
    output = model((species, coordinates))
    predicted_energies = output.energies
    
    if force_training:
        target_forces = batch["forces"].float()
        # Compute forces with gradient tracking
        predicted_forces = forces_for_training(predicted_energies, coordinates)
        
        # Energy loss (normalized by sqrt of number of atoms)
        energy_loss = (mse(predicted_energies, target_energies) / num_atoms.sqrt()).mean()
        
        # Force loss (normalized by number of atoms)
        force_loss = (mse(predicted_forces, target_forces).sum(dim=(1, 2)) / num_atoms).mean()
        
        # Combined loss
        loss = energy_loss + force_coefficient * force_loss
    else:
        loss = (mse(predicted_energies, target_energies) / num_atoms.sqrt()).mean()
    
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
```

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:149-184](), [torchani/grad.py:82-83]()

## Loss Function Construction

### Energy Loss Normalization

Energy losses are typically normalized by the square root of the number of atoms to account for system size:

```
L_energy = MSE(E_pred, E_target) / sqrt(N_atoms)
```

This is implemented at [examples/training.py:172-174]().

### Force Loss Normalization

Force losses are normalized by the number of atoms:

```
L_force = MSE(F_pred, F_target).sum(atoms, xyz) / N_atoms
```

Since forces are per-atom 3D vectors, the MSE is summed over both atom and coordinate dimensions before normalization, as shown at [examples/training.py:175-177]().

### Combined Loss

The total loss combines energy and force terms with a weighting coefficient:

```
L_total = L_energy + λ * L_force
```

Common coefficient values:
- `λ = 0.1` - typical starting point
- `λ = 0.01 to 1.0` - range used in practice depending on dataset

**Loss Function Comparison Table:**

| Loss Component | Shape Before Reduction | Normalization | Typical Weight |
|----------------|------------------------|---------------|----------------|
| Energy Loss | `(molecules,)` | `/ sqrt(num_atoms)` | 1.0 |
| Force Loss | `(molecules, atoms, 3)` | `/ num_atoms` | 0.1 |

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:172-178]()

## Requirements for Force Training

### Coordinate Tensor Requirements

The coordinate tensor must satisfy specific requirements for force computation:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Coords["coordinates Tensor"]
    
    Check1{"is leaf tensor?"}
    Coords --> Check1
    Check1 -->|No| Error1["ValueError:<br/>must be leaf tensor"]
    Check1 -->|Yes| Check2
    
    Check2{"requires_grad?"}
    Check2 -->|No| Error2["ValueError:<br/>must require grad"]
    Check2 -->|Yes| Valid["Valid for<br/>force computation"]
    
    style Error1 fill:#ffe0e0
    style Error2 fill:#ffe0e0
    style Valid fill:#e0ffe0
```

**Validation Logic:**

The `forces` function validates coordinate tensors at [torchani/grad.py:48-56]():

1. **Must require gradients:** `coordinates.requires_grad` must be `True`
2. **Must be a leaf tensor:** `coordinates.is_leaf` must be `True` (not derived from other operations)

These requirements ensure that gradients can be computed and backpropagated correctly.

**Sources:** [torchani/grad.py:48-56]()

## Computational Considerations

### Memory Requirements

Force training requires additional memory for:

1. **Computation graph storage:** `create_graph=True` builds a graph for second-order gradients
2. **Intermediate gradients:** Force vectors for all atoms must be retained
3. **Backward pass through forces:** Additional graph nodes for force loss backpropagation

**Memory scaling:**
- Energy-only training: `O(N_atoms)`
- Force training: `O(N_atoms × 3)` for forces + graph overhead

### Computational Cost

Force computation adds overhead to the training loop:

| Operation | Relative Cost | Notes |
|-----------|---------------|-------|
| Forward pass (energy) | 1× | Base cost |
| Force computation | ~1× | Backward through energy |
| Energy loss backward | 1× | Standard backprop |
| Force loss backward | ~2-3× | Backward through backward |
| **Total with forces** | **~5-6×** | Approximate total overhead |

Despite the increased cost, force training typically:
- Improves model accuracy on forces
- Enhances transferability to new configurations
- Reduces the number of epochs needed for convergence

**Sources:** [torchani/grad.py:82-83](), [examples/training.py:169-184]()

## Testing and Validation

### Force Accuracy Testing

The test suite validates force predictions against reference data:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Test["Test Data"]
    Coords["coordinates"]
    Species["species"]
    RefForces["reference_forces"]
    
    Test --> Coords
    Test --> Species
    Test --> RefForces
    
    Compute["energies_and_forces(model, species, coordinates)"]
    Coords --> Compute
    Species --> Compute
    
    Compute --> PredE["predicted_energies"]
    Compute --> PredF["predicted_forces"]
    
    Compare["assertEqual(predicted_forces, reference_forces)"]
    PredF --> Compare
    RefForces --> Compare
```

**Test Implementation:**

- [tests/test_forces.py:20-30]() tests force accuracy on individual conformers
- [tests/test_forces.py:32-55]() tests force accuracy on padded batches
- [torchani/grad.py:263-291]() implements `energies_and_forces` for validation

**Sources:** [tests/test_forces.py:20-55](), [torchani/grad.py:263-291]()

## Best Practices

### 1. Start with Energy-Only Training

Begin training with energy-only loss to establish baseline convergence, then enable force training:

```python
# Phase 1: Energy-only (epochs 0-50)
force_training = False

# Phase 2: Energy + forces (epochs 50+)
force_training = True
force_coefficient = 0.1
```

### 2. Tune Force Coefficient

The force coefficient balances energy and force contributions:

- **Too low (< 0.01):** Forces under-weighted, poor force accuracy
- **Too high (> 1.0):** Forces dominate, potential energy surface distortion
- **Recommended:** Start with 0.1 and adjust based on validation metrics

### 3. Monitor Both Metrics

Track separate RMSE values for energies and forces during validation:

```python
energy_rmse = sqrt(mean((E_pred - E_target)²))
force_rmse = sqrt(mean((F_pred - F_target)²))
```

### 4. Validate Gradient Computation

Use gradient checking to ensure force implementation is correct:

[tests/test_aev.py:135-163]() demonstrates gradient validation using finite differences vs. autograd.

### 5. Memory Management

For large systems or batches:
- Use gradient checkpointing if available
- Reduce batch size when enabling force training
- Consider mixed precision training (float16 energies, float32 forces)

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:149-184](), [tests/test_aev.py:135-163]()

## Common Implementation Patterns

### Pattern 1: Conditional Force Training

Toggle force training based on epoch or convergence:

```python
if epoch >= force_training_start_epoch:
    predicted_forces = forces_for_training(predicted_energies, coordinates)
    force_loss = compute_force_loss(predicted_forces, target_forces)
    loss = energy_loss + force_coefficient * force_loss
else:
    loss = energy_loss
```

### Pattern 2: Adaptive Force Coefficient

Adjust the force coefficient during training:

```python
# Gradually increase force weight
force_coefficient = min(0.1 * (epoch / 50), 0.5)
```

### Pattern 3: Per-Atom Normalization

Normalize losses by atom count for size-independent training:

```python
num_atoms = (species >= 0).sum(dim=1, dtype=energies.dtype)
energy_loss = mse(pred_energies, target_energies) / num_atoms.sqrt()
force_loss = mse(pred_forces, target_forces).sum(dim=(1,2)) / num_atoms
```

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:166-178]()

## Integration with TorchANI Components

### With ANI Models

Force training works seamlessly with all ANI model variants:

- `ANI1x` - [torchani/models.py]()
- `ANI2x` - [torchani/models.py]()
- `ANI2dr` - [torchani/models.py]()
- Custom models from `Assembler` - see [Building Custom Models](#5.3)

### With Ensemble Models

For ensemble models, forces are computed for the mean energy:

```python
ensemble_output = ensemble_model((species, coordinates))
mean_energy = ensemble_output.energies.mean(dim=0)  # Average over ensemble
forces = forces_for_training(mean_energy, coordinates)
```

**Sources:** [tests/test_ensemble.py:26-37](), [torchani/grad.py:82-83]()

## Summary

Force training in TorchANI requires:

1. **Proper tensor setup:** Coordinates must be leaf tensors with `requires_grad=True`
2. **Specialized computation:** Use `forces_for_training` with `create_graph=True` for double backpropagation
3. **Combined loss:** Weight energy and force losses appropriately
4. **Normalization:** Scale losses by atom count for size-independent training
5. **Validation:** Test both energy and force accuracy

The additional computational cost is offset by improved model quality, better transferability, and enhanced physical accuracy of the learned potential energy surface.

**Sources:** [examples/training.py:149-184](), [torchani/grad.py:42-83](), [tests/test_forces.py:1-59]()

# Page: Advanced Topics

# Advanced Topics

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [.gitignore](.gitignore)
- [README.md](README.md)
- [setup.py](setup.py)
- [torchani/arch.py](torchani/arch.py)
- [torchani/nn/__init__.py](torchani/nn/__init__.py)
- [torchani/nn/_containers.py](torchani/nn/_containers.py)
- [torchani/nn/_core.py](torchani/nn/_core.py)
- [torchani/nn/_infer.py](torchani/nn/_infer.py)
- [torchani/nn/_internal.py](torchani/nn/_internal.py)

</details>



This section covers advanced features, optimizations, and techniques for expert users of TorchANI. The material here assumes familiarity with the core concepts and basic usage patterns described in earlier sections. Topics include performance optimization strategies, compiled extensions, benchmarking tools, and handling of periodic boundary conditions.

For basic model usage and energy calculations, see [User Guide](#5). For training workflows, see [Training](#7).

## Overview

TorchANI provides several advanced capabilities designed for production deployments, high-throughput screening, and specialized research applications:

1. **Performance Optimization** - Techniques to accelerate inference through JIT compilation and inference-optimized model representations
2. **C++ and CUDA Extensions** - Optional compiled extensions that significantly improve computational performance
3. **Benchmarking Tools** - Utilities to measure and compare performance across different configurations
4. **Periodic Boundary Conditions** - Support for crystalline and condensed-phase systems

These features enable TorchANI to scale from exploratory research to production molecular dynamics simulations.

## Performance Optimization Strategies

TorchANI provides multiple optimization paths that can dramatically improve inference speed, particularly for molecular dynamics and high-throughput applications.

### Inference Model Conversion

The standard model architecture prioritizes flexibility and training efficiency. For inference-only applications, models can be converted to optimized representations that reduce Python overhead and improve GPU utilization.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Standard["Standard Model<br/>ANI or Ensemble"]
    ToInfer["to_infer_model()<br/>[arch.py:221-230]"]
    Decision{"use_mnp=?"}
    MNP["MNPNetworks<br/>[nn/_infer.py:219-371]"]
    BMM["BmmEnsemble<br/>[nn/_infer.py:61-130]"]
    
    Standard --> ToInfer
    ToInfer --> Decision
    Decision -->|"True"| MNP
    Decision -->|"False"| BMM
    
    MNP --> Streams["Multi-Stream Execution<br/>Parallel Element Networks"]
    BMM --> Batched["Batched Matrix Ops<br/>Fused Ensemble Members"]
```

**Optimization Approaches:**

| Strategy | Class | Use Case | Performance Gain |
|----------|-------|----------|------------------|
| Batched Matrix Multiplication | `BmmEnsemble` | Ensemble models, single conformer | 2-4x speedup |
| Multi-Net Parallel (Python) | `MNPNetworks` (use_mnp=False) | Testing/debugging | Minimal |
| Multi-Net Parallel (C++) | `MNPNetworks` (use_mnp=True) | Production MD, requires extension | 3-6x speedup |

The `to_infer_model()` method, available on ANI models at [arch.py:221-230](), automatically selects the appropriate optimization strategy:

```python
model = torchani.models.ANI2x()
# Convert to inference-optimized version
infer_model = model.to_infer_model(use_mnp=False)  # BmmEnsemble
# or
infer_model = model.to_infer_model(use_mnp=True)   # MNPNetworks (requires extension)
```

Sources: [torchani/arch.py:221-230](), [torchani/nn/_infer.py:61-371]()

### JIT Compilation

PyTorch's TorchScript JIT compiler can further optimize models by eliminating Python interpreter overhead:

```python
model = torchani.models.ANI2x()
scripted_model = torch.jit.script(model)
```

JIT compilation works with both standard and inference-optimized models. For ASE integration, the `ase()` method accepts a `jit=True` parameter at [arch.py:232-254]().

Sources: [torchani/arch.py:232-254]()

### Network Architecture Optimizations

The inference-optimized classes make specific architectural transformations:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Standard Ensemble"
        E1["Member 1<br/>H-Net, C-Net, N-Net"]
        E2["Member 2<br/>H-Net, C-Net, N-Net"]
        E8["Member 8<br/>H-Net, C-Net, N-Net"]
    end
    
    Transform["BmmEnsemble<br/>Transformation"]
    
    subgraph "Optimized Ensemble"
        BH["BmmAtomicNetwork<br/>8 H-Networks Fused"]
        BC["BmmAtomicNetwork<br/>8 C-Networks Fused"]
        BN["BmmAtomicNetwork<br/>8 N-Networks Fused"]
    end
    
    E1 --> Transform
    E2 --> Transform
    E8 --> Transform
    Transform --> BH
    Transform --> BC
    Transform --> BN
```

The `BmmAtomicNetwork` class at [nn/_infer.py:132-168]() fuses ensemble members for the same element into a single module using batched matrix multiplication. The `BmmLinear` layer at [nn/_infer.py:170-217]() replaces standard linear layers with batched equivalents:

- Standard: Multiple forward passes with shape `(atoms, features)`
- Optimized: Single batched forward pass with shape `(ensemble_size, atoms, features)`

Sources: [torchani/nn/_infer.py:61-217]()

## Extension System Architecture

TorchANI includes three optional C++/CUDA extensions that provide significant performance improvements:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Extensions["C++/CUDA Extensions"]
        cuAEV["cuAEV<br/>CUDA AEV Kernel<br/>[csrc/aev.cu]"]
        MNP["MNP<br/>Multi-Net Parallel<br/>[csrc/mnp.cpp]"]
        CellList["CellList<br/>Neighbor Search<br/>[csrc/cell_list.cpp]"]
    end
    
    subgraph Build["Build Configuration<br/>[setup.py]"]
        Detect["Device Detection<br/>[setup.py:205-220]"]
        Compile["Extension Compilation<br/>[setup.py:43-117]"]
    end
    
    subgraph Runtime["Runtime Selection"]
        Strategy["set_strategy()<br/>[arch.py:153-159]"]
        UseMNP["to_infer_model(use_mnp)<br/>[arch.py:221-230]"]
    end
    
    Detect --> Compile
    Compile --> cuAEV
    Compile --> MNP
    Compile --> CellList
    
    cuAEV --> Strategy
    MNP --> UseMNP
```

**Extension Details:**

| Extension | Language | Functionality | Target |
|-----------|----------|---------------|--------|
| cuAEV | CUDA | Fused AEV computation kernel | GPU |
| MNP | C++ (OpenMP) | Parallel network evaluation | CPU multi-core |
| CellList | C++ (OpenMP) | Spatial hashing neighborlist | CPU multi-core |

The build system at [setup.py:43-289]() automatically detects available CUDA devices and compiles extensions with appropriate compute capabilities. Extensions can be selectively enabled during installation:

```bash
# No extensions
pip install --no-deps -v .

# All extensions (auto-detect GPU)
pip install --config-settings=--global-option=ext --no-build-isolation --no-deps -v .

# All extensions (all GPU architectures)
pip install --config-settings=--global-option=ext-all-sms --no-build-isolation --no-deps -v .
```

Sources: [setup.py:1-289](), [README.md:74-84]()

### Runtime Strategy Selection

Models can switch between Python and CUDA implementations at runtime without reloading:

```python
model = torchani.models.ANI2x()

# Use Python implementation
model.set_strategy("pyaev")

# Use CUDA implementation (if compiled)
model.set_strategy("cuaev")
```

The `set_strategy()` method at [arch.py:153-159]() modifies the AEV computer's computation path. The cuAEV extension can bypass the neighborlist entirely when no additional potentials are present, as seen in the optimized branch at [arch.py:340-362]().

Sources: [torchani/arch.py:153-159](), [torchani/arch.py:340-362]()

### MNP Architecture

The Multi-Net Parallel extension parallelizes network evaluation across element types using OpenMP threads:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    AEV["AEV Input<br/>(molecules, atoms, features)"]
    Split["Species Splitting<br/>[nn/_infer.py:336-338]"]
    
    subgraph Parallel["OpenMP Parallel Region"]
        H["Thread 1<br/>H Atoms"]
        C["Thread 2<br/>C Atoms"]
        N["Thread 3<br/>N Atoms"]
        O["Thread 4<br/>O Atoms"]
    end
    
    Reduce["Sum Reduction"]
    Energy["Total Energy"]
    
    AEV --> Split
    Split --> H
    Split --> C
    Split --> N
    Split --> O
    H --> Reduce
    C --> Reduce
    N --> Reduce
    O --> Reduce
    Reduce --> Energy
```

The `MNPNetworks` class at [nn/_infer.py:219-371]() provides both a Python reference implementation (`PythonMNP` at [nn/_infer.py:381-469]()) and integration with the C++ extension via `torch.ops.mnp.run()` at [nn/_infer.py:359-370]().

MNP requires `OMP_NUM_THREADS >= 2` for optimal performance. The implementation checks this environment variable at [nn/_infer.py:23-36]().

Sources: [torchani/nn/_infer.py:219-469]()

## Benchmarking Capabilities

TorchANI includes benchmarking infrastructure to measure and compare performance across different configurations. While the specific benchmark scripts are not in the provided files, the architecture supports performance measurement through:

1. **NVTX Annotations** - CUDA profiling markers at [nn/_infer.py:120-125]() for identifying bottlenecks
2. **Gradient Computation Testing** - Verification that optimizations preserve correctness
3. **Active Member Selection** - Testing ensemble subsets via `set_active_members()` at [arch.py:137-143]()

The inference-optimized classes include caching mechanisms to avoid redundant computation when processing similar molecular configurations, as seen in the species comparison logic at [nn/_infer.py:112-114]().

Sources: [torchani/nn/_infer.py:112-125](), [torchani/arch.py:137-143]()

## Periodic Boundary Conditions

TorchANI supports periodic boundary conditions for simulating bulk materials, surfaces, and solution-phase systems. PBC handling is integrated throughout the computation pipeline:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input["Input: species, coords, cell, pbc"]
    Wrap["Coordinate Wrapping<br/>Map to Central Cell"]
    Neighbors["Neighborlist Construction<br/>with PBC"]
    
    subgraph "Neighborlist Algorithms"
        AllPairs["AllPairs<br/>No PBC support"]
        CellList["CellList<br/>PBC via cell list<br/>[csrc/cell_list.cpp]"]
        Adaptive["AdaptiveList<br/>Auto-select based on system"]
    end
    
    AEV["AEV Computation<br/>with periodic images"]
    Energy["Energy + Forces"]
    
    Input --> Wrap
    Wrap --> Neighbors
    Neighbors --> AllPairs
    Neighbors --> CellList
    Neighbors --> Adaptive
    
    AllPairs --> AEV
    CellList --> AEV
    Adaptive --> AEV
    
    AEV --> Energy
```

The `forward()` method signature accepts `cell` and `pbc` arguments at [arch.py:325-382](), which are passed through the computation chain. The neighborlist algorithms handle periodic images differently:

| Algorithm | PBC Support | Use Case |
|-----------|-------------|----------|
| AllPairs | No | Small molecules, gas phase |
| CellList | Yes | Large periodic systems |
| AdaptiveList | Yes | Automatic selection |

The ASE calculator integration provides additional PBC utilities:
- Coordinate wrapping to central cell
- Optional position overwriting via `overwrite` parameter at [arch.py:232-254]()
- Multiple stress calculation strategies via `stress_kind` parameter

For external neighborlists (e.g., from MD engines), the `compute_from_external_neighbors()` method at [arch.py:183-219]() handles PBC neighbors with proper screening via `narrow_down()` at [arch.py:205]() to enforce the model's cutoff radius.

Sources: [torchani/arch.py:183-219](), [torchani/arch.py:325-382](), [torchani/arch.py:232-254]()

## Memory and Computational Considerations

Advanced usage often involves trade-offs between memory consumption and computational speed:

**Ensemble Models:**
- Standard `Ensemble`: Lower memory, Python iteration overhead
- `BmmEnsemble`: Higher GPU memory (batched weights), faster execution
- `MNPNetworks`: Similar memory to standard, CPU parallelism overhead

**Single-Conformer Optimization:**
The inference-optimized classes require single-conformer inputs (batch size = 1) as enforced at [nn/_infer.py:109]() and [nn/_infer.py:332](). This constraint enables species-specific caching at [nn/_infer.py:96-98]() and [nn/_infer.py:254-256]().

**Active Member Selection:**
For ensemble models, the `set_active_members()` method at [arch.py:137-143]() allows reducing computational cost by evaluating only a subset of ensemble members without reloading the model.

Sources: [torchani/nn/_infer.py:96-114](), [torchani/nn/_infer.py:254-256](), [torchani/nn/_infer.py:332](), [torchani/arch.py:137-143]()
