# Page: Performance Optimization

# Performance Optimization

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [.gitignore](.gitignore)
- [README.md](README.md)
- [setup.py](setup.py)
- [torchani/arch.py](torchani/arch.py)
- [torchani/nn/__init__.py](torchani/nn/__init__.py)
- [torchani/nn/_containers.py](torchani/nn/_containers.py)
- [torchani/nn/_core.py](torchani/nn/_core.py)
- [torchani/nn/_infer.py](torchani/nn/_infer.py)
- [torchani/nn/_internal.py](torchani/nn/_internal.py)

</details>



This page describes techniques for optimizing the inference speed of TorchANI models. The primary optimization strategies include converting models to inference-optimized versions, using compiled C++/CUDA extensions, JIT compilation, and selecting appropriate AEV computation strategies.

For information about building and installing the C++/CUDA extensions themselves, see [Building Extensions](#2.2). For benchmarking tools to measure performance improvements, see [Benchmarking](#8.3).

---

## Overview of Optimization Strategies

TorchANI provides multiple complementary approaches to improve inference performance:

| Strategy | Speedup | Use Case | Requirements |
|----------|---------|----------|--------------|
| Inference Models (`to_infer_model()`) | 2-3x | Single-molecule inference, MD | None |
| cuAEV Extension | 3-5x | AEV computation | CUDA GPU |
| MNP Extension | 1.5-2x | Multi-network parallelization | CUDA GPU, OpenMP |
| JIT Compilation | 1.2-1.5x | Production inference | None |
| Strategy Selection (`cuaev` vs `pyaev`) | 3-5x | AEV computation | CUDA GPU |

These optimizations can be combined for maximum performance. The most significant gains come from using cuAEV for AEV computation and converting ensembles to `BmmEnsemble` for neural network evaluation.

Sources: [README.md:142-154](), [torchani/arch.py:221-230](), [torchani/nn/_infer.py:1-470]()

---

## Inference Model Conversion

### BmmEnsemble: Batched Matrix Multiplication for Ensembles

The `BmmEnsemble` class converts ensemble models to use batched matrix multiplication (BMM), which significantly reduces Python overhead and CUDA kernel calls.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Standard Ensemble"
        E1["Ensemble<br/>(8 members)"]
        M1["Member 1"]
        M2["Member 2"]
        M3["Member ..."]
        M8["Member 8"]
        E1 --> M1
        E1 --> M2
        E1 --> M3
        E1 --> M8
    end
    
    subgraph "BmmEnsemble"
        BE["BmmEnsemble<br/>(fused)"]
        BH["BmmAtomicNetwork<br/>(H, 8 nets)"]
        BC["BmmAtomicNetwork<br/>(C, 8 nets)"]
        BN["BmmAtomicNetwork<br/>(N, 8 nets)"]
        BE --> BH
        BE --> BC
        BE --> BN
    end
    
    E1 -->|to_infer_model| BE
```

**Optimization Mechanics:**

The conversion from `Ensemble` to `BmmEnsemble` fuses all networks for each element into a single `BmmAtomicNetwork`. Each `BmmAtomicNetwork` contains `BmmLinear` layers that perform batched operations:

```
Input:  (ensemble_size x num_atoms x features)
Weight: (ensemble_size x features x output)
Bias:   (ensemble_size x 1 x output)
Output: (ensemble_size x num_atoms x output)
```

**Usage:**

```python
# Load ensemble model
model = torchani.models.ANI2x()

# Convert to inference model
infer_model = model.to_infer_model(use_mnp=False)

# Now use for inference
energies = infer_model((species, coords))
```

**Implementation Details:**

- [torchani/nn/_containers.py:657-662]() - `Ensemble.to_infer_model()` method
- [torchani/nn/_infer.py:61-130]() - `BmmEnsemble` implementation
- [torchani/nn/_infer.py:132-168]() - `BmmAtomicNetwork` implementation
- [torchani/nn/_infer.py:170-217]() - `BmmLinear` layer using `torch.baddbmm`

**Performance Characteristics:**

The `BmmEnsemble` caches element indices to avoid redundant computations when the same molecular structure is evaluated repeatedly (common in MD simulations):

- [torchani/nn/_infer.py:94-98]() - Index list caching
- [torchani/nn/_infer.py:112-114]() - Same tensor check and index list reuse

Sources: [torchani/nn/_infer.py:61-217](), [torchani/nn/_containers.py:657-662](), [torchani/arch.py:221-230]()

---

### MNPNetworks: Multi-Network Parallel Execution

`MNPNetworks` is an experimental optimization that parallelizes neural network evaluation across multiple CUDA streams and (optionally) uses OpenMP for CPU-side parallelization.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Input Processing"
        AEV["AEV Tensor<br/>(all atoms)"]
        Split["Split by<br/>Element Type"]
        H["H atoms"]
        C["C atoms"]
        N["N atoms"]
        O["O atoms"]
        
        AEV --> Split
        Split --> H
        Split --> C
        Split --> N
        Split --> O
    end
    
    subgraph "Parallel Execution"
        S0["CUDA Stream 0"]
        S1["CUDA Stream 1"]
        S2["CUDA Stream 2"]
        S3["CUDA Stream 3"]
        
        H --> S0
        C --> S1
        N --> S2
        O --> S3
        
        S0 --> Net0["H Network"]
        S1 --> Net1["C Network"]
        S2 --> Net2["N Network"]
        S3 --> Net3["O Network"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Synchronization"
        Sync["Stream Sync"]
        Sum["Sum Energies"]
        
        Net0 --> Sync
        Net1 --> Sync
        Net2 --> Sync
        Net3 --> Sync
        Sync --> Sum
    end
```

**Usage with C++ Extension:**

```python
# Requires MNP extension to be compiled
model = torchani.models.ANI2x()
infer_model = model.to_infer_model(use_mnp=True)

# Set OpenMP threads for best performance
import os
os.environ['OMP_NUM_THREADS'] = '4'

energies = infer_model((species, coords))
```

**Requirements and Limitations:**

- Requires CUDA GPU ([torchani/nn/_infer.py:222-223]())
- Only supports single-conformation inputs ([torchani/nn/_infer.py:332]())
- Does not support atomic energies output ([torchani/nn/_infer.py:333]())
- Requires `OMP_NUM_THREADS` environment variable ([torchani/nn/_infer.py:23-36]())
- Experimental and subject to change ([torchani/nn/_infer.py:226-232]())

**Implementation:**

The C++ implementation uses:
- Multiple CUDA streams for parallel GPU execution ([torchani/nn/_infer.py:259]())
- Flattened weight/bias tensors passed to `torch.ops.mnp.run` ([torchani/nn/_infer.py:351-370]())
- OpenMP for CPU-side parallelization (C++ code in `torchani/csrc/mnp.cpp`)

A Python fallback implementation exists for testing but is not performant ([torchani/nn/_infer.py:381-469]()).

Sources: [torchani/nn/_infer.py:219-371](), [setup.py:83-98](), [README.md:150-153]()

---

## C++/CUDA Extensions

### cuAEV: CUDA-Accelerated AEV Computation

The cuAEV extension provides a fused CUDA kernel for computing Atomic Environment Vectors, which is typically the most computationally expensive part of ANI inference.

**Building cuAEV:**

The extension is built with specific CUDA compute capabilities (SM versions):

```bash
# Build for detected GPUs
pip install --config-settings=--global-option=ext --no-build-isolation --no-deps -v .

# Build for all supported architectures
pip install --config-settings=--global-option=ext-all-sms --no-build-isolation --no-deps -v .

# Build for specific SM (e.g., SM 80 for Ampere)
pip install --config-settings=--global-option=ext-sm80 --no-build-isolation --no-deps -v .
```

**Supported Compute Capabilities:**

| SM Version | Architecture | Generation |
|------------|--------------|------------|
| 60, 61 | Pascal | - |
| 70 | Volta | 1st gen TensorCore |
| 75 | Turing | 2nd gen TensorCore |
| 80, 86 | Ampere | 3rd gen TensorCore |
| 89 | Ada Lovelace, Hopper | 4th gen TensorCore |
| 100 | Blackwell | 5th gen TensorCore |

**Compilation Flags:**

- [setup.py:51-69]() - NVCC compiler arguments including:
  - `--expt-extended-lambda` for lambda support
  - CUB namespace definitions for safety
  - `-DTORCHANI_OPT` and `-use_fast_math` for optimization
  - Architecture-specific `-gencode` flags

**CUB Library:**

For CUDA versions < 12.8, the CUB library is required and automatically downloaded if not found ([setup.py:11-40]()).

**Strategy Selection:**

To use cuAEV, set the strategy:

```python
model.set_strategy('cuaev')  # Use CUDA kernel
model.set_strategy('pyaev')  # Use Python implementation
```

The strategy can be set via the `Assembler` during model construction or changed dynamically at runtime ([torchani/arch.py:153-159]()).

Sources: [setup.py:43-80](), [setup.py:138-147](), [README.md:148-153]()

---

### MNP: Multi-Network Parallel Extension

The MNP (Multi-Net Parallel) extension uses OpenMP to parallelize neural network evaluation across element types.

**Building MNP:**

```bash
pip install --config-settings=--global-option=ext --no-build-isolation --no-deps -v .
```

**Compilation:**

- [setup.py:83-98]() - C++ compiler arguments:
  - `-std=c++17` for C++17 support
  - `-fopenmp` for OpenMP parallelization
  - `-DTORCHANI_DEBUG` (optional debug flag)

**Environment Configuration:**

```bash
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=4  # Or use SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
```

The number of OpenMP threads should be ≥ 2 for best performance ([torchani/nn/_infer.py:27-29]()).

Sources: [setup.py:83-98](), [torchani/nn/_infer.py:23-36]()

---

### CellList: Optimized Neighborlist

The CellList extension provides an optimized C++ implementation of cell-list based neighbor searching, particularly beneficial for large systems with periodic boundary conditions.

**Building CellList:**

Built automatically with the other extensions:

```bash
pip install --config-settings=--global-option=ext --no-build-isolation --no-deps -v .
```

**Compilation:**

- [setup.py:101-116]() - Same compiler flags as MNP
  - `-std=c++17`
  - `-fopenmp`
  - `-DTORCHANI_DEBUG` (optional)

For more details on neighborlist algorithms and when to use CellList, see [Neighborlist Algorithms](#4.3).

Sources: [setup.py:101-116]()

---

## JIT Compilation

TorchANI models can be JIT-compiled using `torch.jit.script()` for additional performance gains, particularly when integrating with ASE:

```python
import torch
import torchani

# Load and optimize model
model = torchani.models.ANI2x()
infer_model = model.to_infer_model()

# JIT compile
jit_model = torch.jit.script(infer_model)

# Use with ASE
calculator = jit_model.ase(jit=False)  # Already JIT-compiled
```

Alternatively, use the `jit=True` flag in the `ase()` method:

```python
calculator = model.ase(jit=True)
```

**JIT Compilation Flow:**

```mermaid
graph LR
    Model["ANI Model"]
    Infer["Inference Model<br/>(to_infer_model)"]
    JIT["JIT Compiled<br/>(torch.jit.script)"]
    ASE["ASE Calculator"]
    
    Model -->|"1. Convert"| Infer
    Infer -->|"2. Compile"| JIT
    JIT -->|"3. Wrap"| ASE
    
    Model -.->|"Direct (jit=True)"| ASE
```

**Benefits:**

- Removes Python interpreter overhead
- Enables graph optimizations
- Reduces memory allocations
- Typical speedup: 1.2-1.5x

**Limitations:**

- Some dynamic Python features not supported
- First call may be slower due to compilation
- Debugging is more difficult

Sources: [torchani/arch.py:232-254]()

---

## Strategy Selection for AEV Computation

The AEV computation strategy has the largest impact on performance. TorchANI supports two strategies:

| Strategy | Implementation | Device | Typical Speedup |
|----------|---------------|--------|-----------------|
| `pyaev` | Python/PyTorch | CPU/GPU | Baseline |
| `cuaev` | Fused CUDA kernel | GPU only | 3-5x |

**Setting Strategy:**

```python
# During model construction
from torchani.arch import Assembler

assembler = Assembler(symbols=('H', 'C', 'N', 'O'))
assembler.set_aev_computer(
    radial=...,
    angular=...,
    strategy='cuaev'  # or 'pyaev'
)
model = assembler.assemble()

# Or dynamically after construction
model.set_strategy('cuaev')
```

**Strategy Dispatch:**

The strategy determines which code path is used:

```mermaid
graph TD
    Input["AEV Computation Request"]
    Check{"Strategy?"}
    
    Input --> Check
    Check -->|"pyaev"| PyImpl["Python Implementation<br/>torchani.aev"]
    Check -->|"cuaev"| CuImpl["CUDA Kernel<br/>torchani.cuaev"]
    
    PyImpl --> Result["AEV Tensors"]
    CuImpl --> Result
```

**Performance Considerations:**

- `cuaev` requires a CUDA GPU and the cuAEV extension to be built
- `cuaev` is always faster on GPU for typical molecular systems
- `pyaev` is the only option for CPU-only systems
- `cuaev` uses fused kernels, reducing memory bandwidth requirements

The strategy is set on the `AEVComputer` instance and can be changed at runtime via `model.set_strategy()` ([torchani/arch.py:153-159]()).

Sources: [torchani/arch.py:750-760]()

---

## Optimization Best Practices

### Recommended Optimization Pipeline

For maximum performance, apply optimizations in this order:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start["Load Model"]
    
    Ext{"cuAEV<br/>installed?"}
    SetStrat["set_strategy('cuaev')"]
    
    Ensemble{"Is Ensemble?"}
    ToInfer["to_infer_model(use_mnp=False)"]
    ToInferMNP["to_infer_model(use_mnp=True)"]
    
    JIT{"Need<br/>JIT?"}
    Compile["torch.jit.script()"]
    
    Use["Use for Inference"]
    
    Start --> Ext
    Ext -->|Yes| SetStrat
    Ext -->|No| Ensemble
    SetStrat --> Ensemble
    
    Ensemble -->|Yes, no MNP| ToInfer
    Ensemble -->|Yes, with MNP| ToInferMNP
    Ensemble -->|No| JIT
    
    ToInfer --> JIT
    ToInferMNP --> JIT
    
    JIT -->|Yes| Compile
    JIT -->|No| Use
    Compile --> Use
```

### Performance Checklist

**For Single-Molecule Inference (MD, Optimization):**

1. ✅ Use `to_infer_model()` if model is an ensemble
2. ✅ Set `strategy='cuaev'` if CUDA GPU available
3. ✅ Consider JIT compilation with `torch.jit.script()`
4. ✅ Use single-conformation inputs (batch size = 1)

**For Batch Inference (Dataset Evaluation):**

1. ✅ Set `strategy='cuaev'` if CUDA GPU available
2. ✅ Keep `to_infer_model()` disabled (or use carefully)
3. ✅ Use larger batch sizes (16-64 conformations)
4. ✅ Consider JIT compilation for very large datasets

**For Ensemble Models:**

1. ✅ Always use `to_infer_model()` → converts to `BmmEnsemble`
2. ✅ Avoid `use_mnp=True` unless benchmarked benefits
3. ✅ Ensure single-conformation inputs for MNP

**For Production Deployment:**

1. ✅ Build all C++/CUDA extensions during installation
2. ✅ Set `OMP_NUM_THREADS` appropriately if using MNP
3. ✅ JIT compile models and save scripted versions
4. ✅ Profile and benchmark specific workloads

Sources: [torchani/nn/_infer.py:1-470](), [torchani/arch.py:221-254](), [README.md:142-154]()

---

## Common Performance Issues

### Issue: Slow Inference Despite GPU Availability

**Symptoms:** Model runs on GPU but performance is poor.

**Causes and Solutions:**

1. **Not using cuAEV:** Check strategy with `model.aev_computer.strategy` and set to `'cuaev'`
2. **Not converted to inference model:** Call `model.to_infer_model()` for ensembles
3. **Large batch sizes with inference model:** `BmmEnsemble` and `MNPNetworks` only support single conformations

### Issue: MNP Performance Worse Than Standard

**Symptoms:** `use_mnp=True` is slower than standard inference.

**Causes and Solutions:**

1. **OMP_NUM_THREADS not set:** Export the environment variable before running
2. **Too few atoms per element:** MNP overhead dominates for small molecules
3. **Using Python MNP fallback:** Ensure C++ extension is installed

### Issue: Out of Memory on GPU

**Symptoms:** CUDA out of memory errors during inference.

**Causes and Solutions:**

1. **Inference model with large batches:** Reduce batch size or don't use inference model
2. **Multiple CUDA streams (MNP):** Each stream requires separate memory allocation
3. **Accumulated gradients:** Use `torch.no_grad()` context for inference

Sources: [torchani/nn/_infer.py:23-36](), [torchani/nn/_infer.py:332-333](), [torchani/arch.py:153-159]()

---

# C++ and CUDA Extensions

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [.gitignore](.gitignore)
- [README.md](README.md)
- [setup.py](setup.py)
- [tests/test_neighbors.py](tests/test_neighbors.py)
- [tools/neighborlist-benchmark.py](tools/neighborlist-benchmark.py)
- [tools/pyaev-benchmark.py](tools/pyaev-benchmark.py)
- [torchani/csrc/CMakeLists.txt](torchani/csrc/CMakeLists.txt)
- [torchani/csrc/__init__.py](torchani/csrc/__init__.py)
- [torchani/csrc/cell_list.cpp](torchani/csrc/cell_list.cpp)
- [torchani/neighbors.py](torchani/neighbors.py)

</details>



This page provides a detailed technical overview of TorchANI's compiled C++ and CUDA extensions, their architecture, build system, and performance characteristics. These extensions are optional but provide significant speedups for production workloads.

For general performance optimization strategies, see [Performance Optimization](#8.1). For benchmarking tools and results, see [Benchmarking](#8.3).

---

## Overview

TorchANI includes three optional compiled extensions that provide substantial performance improvements:

| Extension | Language | Purpose | Typical Speedup |
|-----------|----------|---------|----------------|
| **cuAEV** | CUDA | Fused AEV computation on GPU | 2-5x vs PyTorch |
| **MNP** | C++ (OpenMP) | Parallel neural network evaluation | 2-4x for ensembles |
| **CellList** | C++ | Fast O(N) neighbor list computation | 10-100x for large systems |

All extensions are optional. TorchANI falls back to pure PyTorch implementations when extensions are not available. Extensions are compiled against PyTorch's LibTorch C++ API and registered as custom operators.

**Sources:** [README.md:148-154](), [torchani/csrc/__init__.py:1-60]()

---

## Extension Loading and Detection

Extensions are compiled as shared libraries (`.so` files on Linux) and loaded dynamically at runtime using PyTorch's operator loading mechanism.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Import["Python: import torchani"]
    Init["torchani/csrc/__init__.py"]
    
    LoadCUAEV["torch.ops.load_library(cuaev.so)"]
    LoadMNP["torch.ops.load_library(mnp.so)"]
    LoadCLIST["torch.ops.load_library(cell_list.so)"]
    
    CheckCUAEV{"CUAEV loaded?"}
    CheckMNP{"MNP loaded?"}
    CheckCLIST{"CellList loaded?"}
    
    SetCUAEV["CUAEV_IS_INSTALLED = True"]
    SetMNP["MNP_IS_INSTALLED = True"]
    SetCLIST["CLIST_IS_INSTALLED = True"]
    
    FailCUAEV["CUAEV_IS_INSTALLED = False"]
    FailMNP["MNP_IS_INSTALLED = False"]
    FailCLIST["CLIST_IS_INSTALLED = False"]
    
    WarnCUAEV["warnings.warn(cuAEV not available)"]
    WarnMNP["warnings.warn(MNP not available)"]
    WarnCLIST["warnings.warn(CellList not available)"]
    
    Import --> Init
    Init --> LoadCUAEV
    Init --> LoadMNP
    Init --> LoadCLIST
    
    LoadCUAEV --> CheckCUAEV
    LoadMNP --> CheckMNP
    LoadCLIST --> CheckCLIST
    
    CheckCUAEV -->|Success| SetCUAEV
    CheckCUAEV -->|Exception| FailCUAEV
    CheckMNP -->|Success| SetMNP
    CheckMNP -->|Exception| FailMNP
    CheckCLIST -->|Success| SetCLIST
    CheckCLIST -->|Exception| FailCLIST
    
    FailCUAEV --> WarnCUAEV
    FailMNP --> WarnMNP
    FailCLIST --> WarnCLIST
```

Runtime detection flags are exported as module-level constants:

- `torchani.csrc.CUAEV_IS_INSTALLED`
- `torchani.csrc.MNP_IS_INSTALLED`
- `torchani.csrc.CLIST_IS_INSTALLED`

Warnings can be suppressed by setting the environment variable `TORCHANI_NO_WARN_EXTENSIONS=1`. Extensions can be manually disabled for testing with `TORCHANI_DISABLE_EXTENSIONS=1`.

**Sources:** [torchani/csrc/__init__.py:1-60]()

---

## cuAEV Extension

### Purpose

The `cuAEV` extension implements a fused CUDA kernel for Atomic Environment Vector (AEV) computation. It replaces the pure PyTorch implementation with a highly optimized GPU kernel that computes radial and angular symmetry functions in a single pass.

### Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Python Layer"
        AEVComputer["AEVComputer"]
        Strategy["strategy='cuaev'"]
    end
    
    subgraph "C++ Binding"
        cuaev_cpp["torchani/csrc/cuaev.cpp"]
        Registration["torch::autograd::Function"]
    end
    
    subgraph "CUDA Kernel"
        aev_cu["torchani/csrc/aev.cu"]
        RadialKernel["compute_radial_aevs()"]
        AngularKernel["compute_angular_aevs()"]
        CUB["CUB primitives<br/>cuaev::cub namespace"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Headers"
        aev_h["aev.h<br/>Kernel declarations"]
        cub_h["cuaev_cub.cuh<br/>CUB namespace wrapping"]
    end
    
    AEVComputer --> Strategy
    Strategy --> cuaev_cpp
    cuaev_cpp --> Registration
    Registration --> aev_cu
    
    aev_cu --> RadialKernel
    aev_cu --> AngularKernel
    RadialKernel --> CUB
    AngularKernel --> CUB
    
    cuaev_cpp -.-> aev_h
    aev_cu -.-> aev_h
    aev_cu -.-> cub_h
```

The extension uses custom autograd support to compute gradients efficiently. Unlike the PyTorch implementation which requires gradients through neighbor distances and difference vectors, cuAEV computes gradients directly from coordinates.

### Key Implementation Details

**CUB Library Integration:**
cuAEV requires NVIDIA's CUB library for device-wide reductions and scans. To avoid namespace conflicts with PyTorch's bundled CUB, the extension wraps CUB in a custom namespace:

```cpp
// Namespace definitions from setup.py
-DCUB_NS_QUALIFIER=::cuaev::cub
-DCUB_NS_PREFIX=namespace cuaev {
-DCUB_NS_POSTFIX=}
```

For CUDA 12.8+, CUB is included with CUDA Toolkit and doesn't need separate download. For earlier versions, `setup.py` automatically downloads CUB from GitHub.

**Optimization Flags:**
- `-use_fast_math`: Enables aggressive math optimizations
- `-DTORCHANI_OPT`: Enables intrinsic math functions
- `--expt-extended-lambda`: Required for device lambda functions

**Sources:** [setup.py:11-81](), [torchani/csrc/CMakeLists.txt:36-60]()

### Compute Capability Support

cuAEV supports multiple NVIDIA GPU architectures through the `-gencode` compiler flag. Supported compute capabilities (SMs):

| SM | Architecture | Tensor Cores | Example GPUs |
|----|--------------|--------------|--------------|
| 60, 61 | Pascal | No | GTX 1080, P100 |
| 70 | Volta | 1st gen | V100 |
| 75 | Turing | 2nd gen | RTX 2080, T4 |
| 80, 86 | Ampere | 3rd gen | A100, RTX 3090 |
| 89 | Ada/Hopper | 4th gen | H100, RTX 4090 |
| 100 | Blackwell | 5th gen | Future GPUs |

By default, `setup.py` auto-detects compatible GPUs and compiles only for those architectures. Use `ext-all-sms` flag to compile for all supported architectures (increases compile time significantly).

**Sources:** [setup.py:138-203]()

---

## MNP Extension

### Purpose

MNP (Multi-Net Parallel) is a C++ extension using OpenMP to parallelize neural network evaluations across ensemble members. When using ensemble models (e.g., ANI-2x with 8 networks), MNP evaluates networks in parallel instead of sequentially.

### Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph "Python Layer"
        AtomicContainer["nn.AtomicContainer"]
        Networks["List of ANINetworks"]
    end
    
    subgraph "C++ Extension"
        mnp_cpp["torchani/csrc/mnp.cpp"]
        MNPFunction["MultiNetParallelFunction"]
        OMPParallel["#pragma omp parallel"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Execution"
        Thread0["Thread 0:<br/>Network 0"]
        Thread1["Thread 1:<br/>Network 1"]
        ThreadN["Thread N:<br/>Network N"]
    end
    
    AtomicContainer --> Networks
    Networks -->|"forward()"| mnp_cpp
    mnp_cpp --> MNPFunction
    MNPFunction --> OMPParallel
    
    OMPParallel --> Thread0
    OMPParallel --> Thread1
    OMPParallel --> ThreadN
    
    Thread0 --> Aggregate["Stack results"]
    Thread1 --> Aggregate
    ThreadN --> Aggregate
```

MNP is particularly effective for:
- Ensemble models with 4+ networks
- CPU inference (where parallelism is more beneficial)
- Production deployments where latency matters

On GPU, MNP provides less benefit since GPU parallelism is already efficient for sequential network evaluation.

### Build Configuration

MNP requires:
- C++17 compiler
- OpenMP support (usually available with GCC/Clang)
- PyTorch C++ API (LibTorch)

Compiler flags:
- `-std=c++17`: C++17 standard
- `-fopenmp`: Enable OpenMP
- `-DTORCHANI_DEBUG`: Optional debug symbols

**Sources:** [setup.py:83-98](), [torchani/csrc/CMakeLists.txt:63-73]()

---

## CellList Extension

### Purpose

The CellList extension implements a fast O(N) neighbor list algorithm in C++ with full autograd support. It subdivides space into a 3D grid of "buckets" and only checks pairs within and between neighboring buckets.

### Algorithm Overview

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input["Input: species, coords, cell, pbc"]
    
    ValidateInputs["_validate_inputs()"]
    
    SetupCell{"PBC?"}
    BoundingCell["compute_bounding_cell()<br/>Create minimal bounding cell"]
    UseInputCell["Use input cell"]
    
    SetupGrid["setup_grid()<br/>Subdivide into buckets"]
    
    GridIdx3["coords_to_grid_idx3()<br/>Assign atoms to buckets"]
    FlattenIdx["flatten_idx3()<br/>Convert 3D → 1D index"]
    
    CountAtoms["count_atoms_in_buckets()<br/>Count per bucket"]
    
    ImagePairs["Create image pairs:<br/>- Within buckets<br/>- Between buckets"]
    
    ConvertPairs["Convert image pairs<br/>to atom pairs"]
    
    NarrowDown["narrow_down()<br/>Filter by cutoff"]
    
    Output["Output: neighbor_idxs,<br/>distances, diff_vectors"]
    
    Input --> ValidateInputs
    ValidateInputs --> SetupCell
    SetupCell -->|No| BoundingCell
    SetupCell -->|Yes| UseInputCell
    
    BoundingCell --> SetupGrid
    UseInputCell --> SetupGrid
    
    SetupGrid --> GridIdx3
    GridIdx3 --> FlattenIdx
    FlattenIdx --> CountAtoms
    
    CountAtoms --> ImagePairs
    ImagePairs --> ConvertPairs
    ConvertPairs --> NarrowDown
    NarrowDown --> Output
```

### Grid Subdivision

The grid is set up with approximately one bucket per cutoff distance in each dimension:

```
bucket_length_lower_bound = (spherical_factor * cutoff) + extra_space
grid_shape = floor_divide(cell_lengths, bucket_length_lower_bound)
```

The `spherical_factor` accounts for non-orthogonal cells, ensuring that a sphere of radius `cutoff` fits within bucket neighborhoods.

### Autograd Support

The extension implements custom backward pass for gradient computation:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Forward["CellListFunction::forward()"]
    SaveContext["Save: coords, neighbor_idxs,<br/>distances, diff_vectors"]
    
    Backward["CellListFunction::backward()"]
    GradDistances["grad_distances"]
    GradDiffVectors["grad_diff_vectors"]
    
    NormDiffVec["norm_diff_vectors =<br/>diff_vectors / distances"]
    
    GradIJ["grad_ij = grad_distances * norm_diff_vectors<br/>+ grad_diff_vectors"]
    
    ScatterAdd["index_add_() to accumulate<br/>gradients on coords"]
    
    Forward --> SaveContext
    SaveContext --> Backward
    
    Backward --> GradDistances
    Backward --> GradDiffVectors
    
    GradDistances --> NormDiffVec
    GradDiffVectors --> NormDiffVec
    
    NormDiffVec --> GradIJ
    GradIJ --> ScatterAdd
```

Gradients are accumulated using `index_add_` for neighbor pairs (i,j):
- `grad_coords[i] += grad_ij`
- `grad_coords[j] -= grad_ij`

**Sources:** [torchani/csrc/cell_list.cpp:274-348](), [torchani/neighbors.py:417-467]()

### FastCellList vs CellList

Two implementations exist:

| Implementation | File | Forward | Backward | Usage |
|---------------|------|---------|----------|-------|
| `CellList` | `neighbors.py` | Pure Python | PyTorch autograd | Default |
| `FastCellList` | `cell_list.cpp` | C++ | Custom C++ | Experimental |

The C++ `FastCellList` uses the same algorithm but implements both forward and backward passes in C++, avoiding Python overhead. It requires the compiled extension.

**Sources:** [torchani/neighbors.py:280-298](), [torchani/csrc/cell_list.cpp:1-372](), [tests/test_neighbors.py:26-64]()

---

## Build System

TorchANI supports two build approaches: pip-based (using `setup.py`) and CMake-based (using `CMakeLists.txt`).

### pip/setuptools Build

The `setup.py` script provides a high-level interface with custom flags:

```bash
# Auto-detect compatible GPUs and build extensions
pip install --config-settings=--global-option=ext --no-build-isolation --no-deps -v .

# Build for all supported GPUs (slower)
pip install --config-settings=--global-option=ext-all-sms --no-build-isolation --no-deps -v .

# Build for specific GPU architecture (e.g., SM 80 for A100)
pip install --config-settings=--global-option=ext-sm80 --no-build-isolation --no-deps -v .

# Build with debug symbols
pip install --config-settings=--global-option=ext --config-settings=--global-option=ext-debug --no-build-isolation --no-deps -v .

# Build without math optimizations
pip install --config-settings=--global-option=ext --config-settings=--global-option=ext-no-opt --no-build-isolation --no-deps -v .
```

#### Build Flags

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `ext` | Build extensions, auto-detect GPU architectures |
| `ext-all-sms` | Build for all supported GPU architectures |
| `ext-sm{XX}` | Build for specific architecture (e.g., `ext-sm80`) |
| `ext-debug` | Enable debug symbols (`-DTORCHANI_DEBUG`) |
| `ext-no-opt` | Disable math optimizations |

#### Requirements

Building extensions requires:
- PyTorch with CUDA support (for cuAEV)
- Compatible CUDA Toolkit (version matching PyTorch)
- C++17 compiler (GCC/Clang)
- OpenMP (for MNP)
- CMake 3.22+ (indirect dependency)

The `--no-build-isolation` flag is **required** because the build needs access to the installed PyTorch and CUDA libraries. The `--no-deps` flag prevents reinstalling PyTorch.

**Sources:** [setup.py:1-289](), [README.md:73-90]()

### CMake Build

For direct CMake builds:

```bash
mkdir build && cd build
cmake .. -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build . --config Release
cmake --install .
```

The CMake build:
1. Auto-detects installed PyTorch location
2. Finds CUDA Toolkit (if available)
3. Configures OpenMP (for MNP)
4. Builds all three extensions
5. Installs to `torchani/` directory

#### CMake Targets

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "CMake Targets"
        cuaev["cuaev target"]
        mnp["mnp target"]
        cell_list["cell_list target"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Dependencies"
        Torch["find_package(Torch)"]
        Python["find_package(Python)"]
        OpenMP["find_package(OpenMP)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Source Files"
        cuaev_cpp["cuaev.cpp"]
        aev_cu["aev.cu"]
        aev_h["aev.h"]
        
        mnp_cpp["mnp.cpp"]
        
        clist_cpp["cell_list.cpp"]
    end
    
    Torch --> cuaev
    Torch --> mnp
    Torch --> cell_list
    
    Python --> cuaev
    Python --> mnp
    Python --> cell_list
    
    OpenMP --> mnp
    
    cuaev_cpp --> cuaev
    aev_cu --> cuaev
    aev_h --> cuaev
    
    mnp_cpp --> mnp
    
    clist_cpp --> cell_list
```

Key CMake configuration:
- Extensions built as shared libraries (`.so`)
- `PREFIX` set to empty string (removes `lib` prefix)
- C++17 standard required
- CUDA compilation with `-use_fast_math` and custom CUB namespace

**Sources:** [torchani/csrc/CMakeLists.txt:1-113]()

### Conda Build

The conda recipe in `recipe/meta.yaml` uses the system CUDA Toolkit and builds extensions by default. It assumes CUDA Toolkit is available at `/usr/local/cuda`.

**Sources:** [README.md:206-242]()

---

## Performance Characteristics

### cuAEV Performance

Typical speedups over PyTorch AEV implementation:
- **Forward pass**: 2-3x faster
- **Backward pass**: 3-5x faster
- **Combined**: 2.5-4x faster

Performance scales with:
- Number of atoms (better for 100+ atoms)
- GPU compute capability (better on newer GPUs)
- Neighbor list density (better for denser systems)

### MNP Performance

Speedups depend on:
- Number of ensemble members (linear scaling expected)
- CPU core count
- Network size
- CPU vs GPU device

Typical speedups for 8-network ensemble on CPU:
- **4 cores**: ~2-3x
- **8 cores**: ~3-4x
- **16+ cores**: ~4-5x

On GPU, MNP provides minimal benefit (<1.2x) since GPU already parallelizes well.

### CellList Performance

Asymptotic complexity:
- **AllPairs**: O(N²)
- **CellList**: O(N)

Crossover point (where CellList becomes faster):
- **With PBC**: ~190 atoms
- **Without PBC**: ~1770 atoms

For very large systems (1000+ atoms), CellList can be 10-100x faster than AllPairs.

**Sources:** [torchani/neighbors.py:327-343](), [tools/neighborlist-benchmark.py:1-209](), [tools/pyaev-benchmark.py:1-231]()

---

## Validation and Testing

All extensions are tested against their pure PyTorch equivalents to ensure numerical accuracy:

### Gradient Verification

The test suite verifies that gradients computed by extensions match PyTorch's autograd:

```python
# From test_neighbors.py
def testGradEqualDistances(self):
    coordsc = self.mc.coords.requires_grad_(True)
    coordsf = self.mf.coords.requires_grad_(True)
    self.clist(..., coordsc).distances.sum().backward()
    self.flist(..., coordsf).distances.sum().backward()
    self.assertEqual(coordsc.grad, coordsf.grad)
```

Tests verify:
- Distance gradients match
- Difference vector gradients match
- Combined gradients match (requires double precision)
- Energy gradients match
- Force gradients match

### Numerical Accuracy

Tests compare:
- AEV values (cuAEV vs PyAEV)
- Neighbor lists (CellList vs AllPairs)
- Energy predictions
- Force predictions

Tolerance is typically:
- `rtol=1e-7, atol=1e-7` for double precision
- `rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-4` for single precision

Float32 has slightly looser tolerances due to non-deterministic operation ordering in CUDA.

**Sources:** [tests/test_neighbors.py:26-482]()

---

## Troubleshooting

### Extension Not Loading

Check the installation flags:
```python
import torchani.csrc
print(f"cuAEV: {torchani.csrc.CUAEV_IS_INSTALLED}")
print(f"MNP: {torchani.csrc.MNP_IS_INSTALLED}")
print(f"CellList: {torchani.csrc.CLIST_IS_INSTALLED}")
```

Common issues:
1. **CUDA version mismatch**: PyTorch CUDA version must match CUDA Toolkit version used for compilation
2. **Missing dependencies**: Ensure CUDA Toolkit dev libraries are installed
3. **Incompatible compiler**: GCC version must support C++17 and be compatible with CUDA

### Build Failures

**CUB not found** (CUDA < 12.8):
- Automatic download should work
- Manual: Download from https://github.com/NVIDIA/cub and place in `include/cub/`

**NVCC version mismatch**:
- Pin `nvcc` version in conda environment to match PyTorch's CUDA version
- See `environment.yaml` for version constraints

**LibTorch not found**:
- Ensure PyTorch is installed before building
- Use `--no-build-isolation` with pip

### Runtime Errors

**Cell too small for PBC**:
- CellList requires cell dimensions > cutoff
- Use AllPairs for small cells with PBC

**SM not supported**:
- Rebuild with correct SM flags for your GPU
- Use `ext-all-sms` to support all GPUs

**Sources:** [torchani/csrc/__init__.py:29-57](), [README.md:184-204]()

## Purpose and Scope

This page documents the benchmarking tools provided in TorchANI for measuring performance and scaling characteristics of different components. These tools enable systematic performance analysis for training workflows, AEV computation, neural network inference, and molecular dynamics simulations. For optimization techniques based on benchmark results, see [Performance Optimization](#8.1). For details on the C++ and CUDA extensions that affect performance, see [C++ and CUDA Extensions](#8.2).

**Sources:** [tools/training-benchmark.py:1-203](), [tools/training-aev-benchmark.py:1-311](), [tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py:1-608](), [tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py:1-351]()

## Overview of Benchmark Tools

TorchANI provides four specialized benchmarking scripts in the `tools/` directory, each targeting different performance aspects:

| Script | Purpose | Key Metrics |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `training-benchmark.py` | Training loop performance | Forward/backward pass timing, component-level profiling |
| `training-aev-benchmark.py` | AEV computation during training | cuAEV vs pyAEV comparison, memory usage |
| `scaling-aev-benchmark.py` | AEV scaling with system size | Performance vs molecule size, speedup analysis |
| `scaling-md-benchmark.py` | MD simulation scaling | Walltime per ns, neighborlist performance |

**Sources:** [tools/training-benchmark.py:1-10](), [tools/training-aev-benchmark.py:1-20](), [tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py:1-20](), [tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py:1-20]()

## Benchmark Tool Architecture


## Training Benchmark

The training benchmark (`training-benchmark.py`) profiles the complete training loop including data loading, forward pass, loss computation, and backward pass. It supports both regular and JIT-compiled models.

### Usage

```bash
# Basic training benchmark with default TestData dataset
python tools/training-benchmark.py

# Benchmark on specific dataset with detailed component profiling
python tools/training-benchmark.py ANI1x --detail --batch-size 2560

# Profile with NVIDIA Nsight Systems
python tools/training-benchmark.py --nvtx --num-warm-up 50 --num-profile 20

# CPU benchmarking (not recommended for performance)
python tools/training-benchmark.py --device cpu
```

### Command-Line Arguments

| Argument | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `dataset` | str | `TestData` | Name of built-in dataset to train on |
| `-d, --device` | str | `cuda`/`cpu` | Device for computation |
| `-w, --num-warm-up` | int | `100` | Number of warm-up batches before profiling |
| `-e, --num-profile` | int | `10` | Number of batches to profile |
| `-b, --batch-size` | int | `2560` | Conformations per batch |
| `--nvtx` | flag | `False` | Emit NVTX markers for Nsight Systems |
| `--no-sync` | flag | `False` | Disable CUDA synchronization |
| `--detail` | flag | `False` | Include component-level timing breakdown |
| `--no-tqdm` | flag | `False` | Disable progress bar |

**Sources:** [tools/training-benchmark.py:108-177]()

### Benchmark Workflow

```mermaid
graph TD
    Start["Load Model & Dataset"] --> WarmUp["Warm-up Phase<br/>num_warm_up batches"]
    WarmUp --> StartProfile["timer.start_profiling"]
    StartProfile --> ProfileLoop["Profile Loop<br/>num_profile batches"]
    
    ProfileLoop --> PrepBatch["timer: prepare-batch<br/>Move data to device"]
    PrepBatch --> ForwardPass["timer: loss-fw<br/>Model forward + loss"]
    ForwardPass --> Backward["timer: loss-bw<br/>loss.backward"]
    Backward --> Optimizer["timer: optimizer<br/>optimizer.step"]
    
    Optimizer --> CheckDone{Done?}
    CheckDone -->|No| ProfileLoop
    CheckDone -->|Yes| StopProfile["timer.stop_profiling"]
    
    StopProfile --> Display["timer.display<br/>Print results"]
    
    style PrepBatch fill:#f9f9f9
    style ForwardPass fill:#f9f9f9
    style Backward fill:#f9f9f9
    style Optimizer fill:#f9f9f9
```

**Sources:** [tools/training-benchmark.py:17-105]()

### Component-Level Profiling

When the `--detail` flag is enabled, the benchmark profiles individual components:

- `model.forward` - Complete model forward pass
- `aev_computer.forward` - AEV computation
- `aev_computer.neighborlist.forward` - Neighborlist construction
- `aev_computer.radial.forward` - Radial symmetry functions
- `aev_computer.angular.forward` - Angular symmetry functions
- `neural_networks.forward` - Neural network inference
- `energy_shifter.forward` - Self-energy addition

**Sources:** [tools/training-benchmark.py:49-58]()

### Example Output

```
Profiling with optimization=NONE, on device: CUDA
NVTX DISABLED
CUDA sync ENABLED

Warm up: 100 batches
Profiling: 10 batches

Timer Results:
  prepare-batch: 12.3 ms
  loss-fw: 45.6 ms
  loss-bw: 78.9 ms
  optimizer: 5.2 ms
  
  model.forward: 38.4 ms
  aev_computer.forward: 25.1 ms
  neural_networks.forward: 10.2 ms
```

**Sources:** [tools/training-benchmark.py:29-32]()

## AEV Training Benchmark

The AEV training benchmark (`training-aev-benchmark.py`) specifically compares `cuAEV` (CUDA extension) and `pyAEV` (PyTorch implementation) performance during training workflows.

### Usage

```bash
# Compare cuAEV vs pyAEV for energy-only training
python tools/training-aev-benchmark.py ANI1x --batch_size 2560 --num_epochs 1

# Include force training benchmark
python tools/training-aev-benchmark.py TestDataForcesDipoles

# Profile with Nsight Systems
python tools/training-aev-benchmark.py --nsight
```

### Command-Line Arguments

| Argument | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `dataset` | str | `ANI1x` | Dataset name (ANI1x or TestDataForcesDipoles) |
| `-d, --device` | str | `cuda`/`cpu` | Device for computation |
| `-b, --batch_size` | int | `2560` | Conformations per batch |
| `-p, --pickle` | flag | `False` | Dataset is pickled |
| `--nsight` | flag | `False` | Enable Nsight profiling |
| `-n, --num_epochs` | int | `1` | Number of epochs to run |

**Sources:** [tools/training-aev-benchmark.py:220-247]()

### Benchmark Execution Flow

```mermaid

    Test2 --> HasForces{Dataset has<br/>forces?}

    HasForces -->|No| Summary
    
    Test3 --> Test4["Test 4: pyAEV Energy + Force Training"]

    end

```

**Sources:** [tools/training-aev-benchmark.py:266-310]()

### Benchmark Implementation

The benchmark function measures separate timing for each component:

```python
# From tools/training-aev-benchmark.py:71-218
# Key timing points:
# 1. AEV forward: aev = aev_computer(species, coordinates)
# 2. NN forward: _, predicted_energies = nn((species, aev))
# 3. Force computation: forces = -torch.autograd.grad(...)
# 4. Backward: loss.backward()
```

**Sources:** [tools/training-aev-benchmark.py:92-168]()

## AEV Scaling Benchmark

The AEV scaling benchmark (`scaling-aev-benchmark.py`) analyzes how AEV computation performance scales with molecular system size. It generates plots showing performance vs. number of atoms.

### Usage

```bash
# Generate scaling plots for AEV computation only
python tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py --plot -N 200

# Include neural network inference
python tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py --plot --run_energy

# Include inference model optimization
python tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py --plot --run_energy --infer_model

# Include MNP (Multi Net Parallel) extension
python tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py --plot --run_energy --infer_model --mnp

# Benchmark single neural network instead of ensemble
python tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py --plot --run_energy --single_nn

# Use cell list for reference pyAEV implementation
python tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py --plot --use-cell-list

# Profile with Nsight Systems
python tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py --nsight
```

### Command-Line Arguments

| Argument | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `-s, --nsight` | flag | `False` | Use Nsight profiling |
| `-p, --plot` | flag | `False` | Generate benchmark plots |
| `-e, --run_energy` | flag | `False` | Run NN to predict energy |
| `--single_nn` | flag | `False` | Use single NN instead of ensemble |
| `--infer_model` | flag | `False` | Use inference model optimization |
| `--mnp` | flag | `False` | Use MNP extension |
| `-n, --N` | int | `200` | Number of repetitions |
| `--use-cell-list` | flag | `False` | Use cell list for pyAEV |
| `--ref-strategy` | str | `pyaev` | Reference strategy (pyaev or cuaev) |

**Sources:** [tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py:492-547]()

### Benchmark Workflow for Plotting

```mermaid
graph TD
    Start["Load Models<br/>ANI2x with pyAEV & cuAEV"] --> LoadPDB["Load PDB File<br/>Extract species & positions"]
    
    LoadPDB --> SizesLoop["For each system size"]
    
    SizesLoop --> ForwardOnly["Benchmark Forward Only<br/>N=200 repetitions"]
    ForwardOnly --> StoreForward["Store forward times"]
    
    StoreForward --> NextSize1{More sizes?}
    NextSize1 -->|Yes| SizesLoop
    NextSize1 -->|No| BackwardLoop["For each system size"]
    
    BackwardLoop --> ForwardBack["Benchmark Forward + Backward<br/>N=200 repetitions"]
    ForwardBack --> StoreBackward["Store forward+backward times"]
    
    StoreBackward --> NextSize2{More sizes?}
    NextSize2 -->|Yes| BackwardLoop
    NextSize2 -->|No| Plot["Generate Plots<br/>matplotlib"]
    
    Plot --> SavePlot["Save PNG & Display"]
    
    subgraph "Each Benchmark Measures"
        PerfVsSize["Performance vs System Size"]
        Speedup["cuAEV vs pyAEV Speedup"]
        ErrorCheck["Numerical Error Validation"]
        MemUsage["GPU Memory Usage"]
    end
    
    style ForwardOnly fill:#f9f9f9
    style ForwardBack fill:#f9f9f9
```

**Sources:** [tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py:468-488]()

### Benchmark Function

The core benchmark function measures performance for a single system size:

**Sources:** [tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py:132-260]()

### Error Validation

**Sources:** [tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py:262-284]()

### Plot Generation

The benchmark generates publication-quality plots showing:

1. **Performance curves**: Time (ms) vs. system size (atoms) for both forward and forward+backward passes

## MD Scaling Benchmark

The MD scaling benchmark (`scaling-md-benchmark.py`) measures molecular dynamics performance scaling with system size using ASE's Langevin dynamics.

### Usage

```bash
# Basic MD scaling benchmark
python tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py -x /path/to/xyz/files -s 100

# Test cell list performance
python tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py -x /path/to/xyz/files --cell-list

# Test Verlet cell list (reuse neighborlist)
python tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py -x /path/to/xyz/files --verlet-cell-list

# Use different model
python tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py -x /path/to/xyz/files -m ani2x

# JIT compilation
python tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py -x /path/to/xyz/files -j

# Generate plots from saved data
python tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py --plot -f ani1x_clist.pkl

# Plot multiple results
python tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py --path-to-files ./tools/plots/
```

### Command-Line Arguments

| Argument | Type | Default | Description |
|----------|------|---------|-------------|
| `-j, --jit` | flag | `False` | Use JIT compilation |
| `-m, --model` | str | `ani1x` | Model name (ani1x, ani2x, ani1ccx) |
| `-d, --device` | str | `cuda` | Device for computation |
| `-s, --steps` | int | `100` | MD timesteps to run |
| `--no-pbc` | flag | `False` | Disable periodic boundary conditions |
| `--model-index` | int | `None` | Specific model index |
| `-x, --xyz` | str | Required | Path to directory with xyz files |
| `-t, --trials` | int | `1` | Number of trials for std dev |
| `-b, --box-repeats` | int | `15` | Box replications in all directions |
| `--cell-list` | flag | `False` | Use cell list neighborlist |
| `--verlet-cell-list` | flag | `False` | Reuse cell list (Verlet) |
| `-p, --plot` | flag | `False` | Generate plots |
| `-f, --file-name` | str | Auto | Output file name |
| `-F, --path-to-files` | str | `None` | Path to multiple result files |

**Sources:** [tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py:158-204]()

### Benchmark Workflow

```mermaid
graph TD
    Start["Load Model & XYZ Files"] --> SortFiles["Sort files by system size"]
    SortFiles --> TrialLoop["For each trial"]
    
    TrialLoop --> FileLoop["For each XYZ file"]
    FileLoop --> ResetTimer["Reset timers"]
    ResetTimer --> CreateAtoms["Create ASE Atoms object<br/>with calculator"]
    
    CreateAtoms --> CreateDyn["Create Langevin dynamics<br/>1 fs timestep, 300K"]
    CreateDyn --> RunMD["Run MD for N steps<br/>dyn.run(steps)"]
    
    RunMD --> MeasureTime["Measure total walltime"]
    MeasureTime --> CollectTimers["Collect component timers"]
    
    CollectTimers --> NextFile{More files?}
    NextFile -->|Yes| FileLoop
    NextFile -->|No| NextTrial{More trials?}
    
    NextTrial -->|Yes| TrialLoop
    NextTrial -->|No| SaveResults["Save results<br/>pickle & CSV"]
    
    SaveResults --> GenPlots["Generate plots<br/>if requested"]
    
    subgraph "Component Timers Tracked"
        FwdTime["forward"]
        BwdTime["backward"]
        NeighborTime["neighborlist"]
        AEVTime["aev_forward"]
    end
    
    style RunMD fill:#f9f9f9
    style CollectTimers fill:#f9f9f9
```

**Sources:** [tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py:234-350]()

### Timer Injection

The benchmark injects timing wrappers into model methods to track individual components:

**Sources:** [tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py:253-279]()

### Output Files

The benchmark generates two types of output files:

1. **Pickle files** (`.pkl`): Complete timing data including all trials, raw times, and component timers
2. **CSV files** (`.csv`): Formatted data with headers for easy analysis

**Sources:** [tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py:328-350]()

### Plot Generation

The benchmark generates plots showing:

1. **Walltime per ns**: Total time to simulate 1 nanosecond vs. system size
2. **Performance**: ns/day (inverse of walltime) vs. system size
3. **Component breakdown**: Separate plots for forward, backward, neighborlist, and AEV times
4. **Error bars**: Standard deviation across multiple trials
5. **Comparison**: Different configurations (cell list vs. all pairs, etc.)

**Sources:** [tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py:21-134]()

## Common Benchmarking Utilities

### CUDA Synchronization

For accurate GPU timing, benchmarks use `torch.cuda.synchronize()` to ensure kernel completion before measuring time:

**Sources:** [tools/training-aev-benchmark.py:50-52](), [tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py:36-38](), [tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py:262-267]()

### NVTX Markers

NVTX (NVIDIA Tools Extension) markers enable detailed profiling with NVIDIA Nsight Systems:

```python
# Enable NVTX profiling
torch.cuda.profiler.start()

# Mark regions of interest
torch.cuda.nvtx.range_push("region_name")
# ... code to profile ...
torch.cuda.nvtx.range_pop()

torch.cuda.profiler.stop()
```

**Sources:** [tools/training-aev-benchmark.py:75-76](), [tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py:305-344](), [tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py:567-607]()

### GPU Memory Tracking

Benchmarks track GPU memory usage using two methods:

1. **PyTorch memory tracking**: `torch.cuda.memory_reserved()` and `torch.cuda.get_device_properties()`
2. **NVIDIA Management Library**: `pynvml` for actual device memory usage

**Sources:** [tools/training-aev-benchmark.py:19-43](), [tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py:23-65]()

### Timer Utility

The `Timer` class (from `tool_utils`) provides:
- Hierarchical timing of code regions
- NVTX integration for Nsight profiling
- Optional CUDA synchronization
- Automatic result display

**Sources:** [tools/training-benchmark.py:12](), [tools/training-benchmark.py:48-64]()

## Performance Analysis Guidelines

### Interpreting Results

When analyzing benchmark results, consider:

1. **Warm-up phase**: First iterations may be slower due to kernel compilation and memory allocation
2. **CUDA synchronization**: Always enable for accurate timing (disable only for Nsight profiling)
3. **Batch size effects**: Larger batches improve GPU utilization but require more memory
4. **Component breakdown**: Identify bottlenecks by examining individual component timings
5. **Speedup ratios**: Compare cuAEV vs pyAEV to quantify CUDA extension benefits

### Common Benchmarking Patterns

**Energy-only vs. Force training:**
- Force training requires backpropagation through the AEV computation
- Expected overhead: 2-3x for force training vs. energy-only training

**System size scaling:**
- AEV computation: O(N²) for all pairs, O(N) for cell list
- Should show linear scaling with cell list for large systems
- Superlinear scaling indicates memory bandwidth issues

**cuAEV speedup:**
- Typical speedup: 3-5x for forward pass
- Higher speedup for larger systems (better GPU utilization)
- Diminishing returns for very small systems (<1000 atoms)

**Sources:** [tools/training-aev-benchmark.py:71-218](), [tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py:262-284]()

### Profiling Best Practices

1. **Use sufficient warm-up**: At least 50-100 iterations to stabilize performance
2. **Run multiple trials**: Calculate mean and standard deviation across trials
3. **Control for system load**: Close other GPU applications during benchmarking
4. **Match production settings**: Use realistic batch sizes and model configurations
5. **Enable detailed profiling**: Use `--detail` or NVTX markers to identify bottlenecks
6. **Validate correctness**: Always verify numerical accuracy when comparing implementations

**Sources:** [tools/training-benchmark.py:65-102](), [tools/scaling-aev-benchmark.py:132-284](), [tools/scaling-md-benchmark.py:253-327]()

# Page: Periodic Boundary Conditions

# Periodic Boundary Conditions

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [tests/test_aev.py](tests/test_aev.py)
- [tests/test_energies.py](tests/test_energies.py)
- [tests/test_ensemble.py](tests/test_ensemble.py)
- [tests/test_forces.py](tests/test_forces.py)
- [tests/test_neighbors.py](tests/test_neighbors.py)
- [tools/neighborlist-benchmark.py](tools/neighborlist-benchmark.py)
- [tools/pyaev-benchmark.py](tools/pyaev-benchmark.py)
- [torchani/csrc/CMakeLists.txt](torchani/csrc/CMakeLists.txt)
- [torchani/csrc/__init__.py](torchani/csrc/__init__.py)
- [torchani/csrc/cell_list.cpp](torchani/csrc/cell_list.cpp)
- [torchani/neighbors.py](torchani/neighbors.py)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

This page describes how TorchANI handles periodic boundary conditions (PBC) for simulating bulk systems and crystals. PBC allows modeling infinite systems by replicating a finite unit cell in three dimensions. The implementation ensures that atoms near cell boundaries can interact with periodic images of atoms on opposite boundaries.

For information about neighborlist algorithms in general, see [Neighborlist Algorithms](#4.3). For AEV computation details, see [AEV Computation](#4.2).

## Concepts and Representation

### Periodic Boundary Conditions

Periodic boundary conditions simulate an infinite system by treating the simulation cell as if it were surrounded by identical copies of itself in all directions. When an atom moves out of one side of the cell, its periodic image enters from the opposite side. This is essential for modeling bulk materials, liquids, and crystals without surface effects.

### Cell and PBC Tensors

TorchANI represents periodic systems using two key tensors:

| Parameter | Type | Shape | Description |
|-----------|------|-------|-------------|
| `cell` | `Tensor` (float) | `(3, 3)` | Unit cell vectors as rows. Each row is a cell basis vector. |
| `pbc` | `Tensor` (bool) | `(3,)` | Whether PBC is enabled along each cell vector direction. |

The `cell` tensor defines the parallelepiped unit cell. For orthogonal cells, it is diagonal. For non-orthogonal cells (triclinic, monoclinic), it contains off-diagonal elements. The `pbc` tensor allows selective application of PBC along different dimensions.

**Sources:** [torchani/neighbors.py:148-165]()

### Minimum Image Convention

TorchANI uses the minimum image convention: when computing distances between atoms, it considers all periodic images and uses the shortest distance. This is implemented through shift vectors that represent which periodic image to use.

## Implementation Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Input["Input: species, coords, cell, pbc"]
    MapCentral["map_to_central\nWrap coords to central cell"]
    
    Input --> CheckPBC{PBC enabled?}
    CheckPBC -->|Yes| MapCentral
    CheckPBC -->|No| NoPBC["Standard computation\nNo shift vectors"]
    
    MapCentral --> CalcShifts["Calculate shift vectors\n_all_pairs_pbc_shifts"]
    CalcShifts --> GenPairs["Generate neighbor pairs\nwith shifts"]
    GenPairs --> ApplyShifts["Apply shifts to\ndiff_vectors"]
    ApplyShifts --> ComputeDist["Compute distances\nusing minimum image"]
    
    NoPBC --> ComputeNoPBC["Compute pairs\nwithout shifts"]
    
    ComputeDist --> Output["Neighbors:\nindices, distances, diff_vectors"]
    ComputeNoPBC --> Output
    
    style MapCentral fill:#f9f9f9
    style CalcShifts fill:#f9f9f9
    style ApplyShifts fill:#f9f9f9
```

**PBC Processing Flow**

When PBC is enabled, coordinates are first mapped to the central cell, shift vectors are calculated to account for periodic images, and distances are computed using the minimum image convention.

**Sources:** [torchani/neighbors.py:189-214](), [torchani/neighbors.py:217-244]()

## Coordinate Mapping to Central Cell

### map_to_central Function

The `map_to_central` function ensures all atomic coordinates lie within the central unit cell. This is critical for PBC calculations to work correctly.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Coords["coords\n(molecules, atoms, 3)"]
    Cell["cell\n(3, 3)"]
    PBC["pbc\n(3,)"]
    
    Coords --> Frac["Fractionalize:\ncoords @ cell.inverse()"]
    Frac --> Wrap["Wrap to [0, 1):\ntorch.remainder(..., 1.0)"]
    Wrap --> Cartesian["Convert to Cartesian:\nfrac @ cell"]
    
    Cell --> Frac
    Cell --> Cartesian
    PBC --> Wrap
    
    Cartesian --> Output["Wrapped coords"]
    
    style Frac fill:#f9f9f9
    style Wrap fill:#f9f9f9
```

**Coordinate Wrapping Process**

The mapping converts coordinates to fractional coordinates (relative to cell vectors), wraps them to the range [0, 1), then converts back to Cartesian coordinates.

**Sources:** [torchani/neighbors.py:10](), [torchani/csrc/cell_list.cpp:9-14]()

The function handles edge cases where coordinates have very small negative values or values slightly greater than 1.0 due to floating-point precision. The C++ implementation includes explicit corrections for these cases:

[torchani/csrc/cell_list.cpp:122-125]()

## Neighborlist Algorithms with PBC

### AllPairs with PBC

The `AllPairs` neighborlist supports PBC by considering all relevant periodic images of the unit cell. The algorithm:

1. Determines which periodic images are needed based on the cutoff radius
2. Generates all atom pairs within the central cell
3. Generates pairs between central cell atoms and periodic images
4. Applies shift vectors to account for periodic translations

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start["all_pairs with PBC"]
    
    Start --> CalcShifts["_all_pairs_pbc_shifts\nDetermine required cell replicas"]
    CalcShifts --> CenterPairs["Generate pairs\nwithin central cell"]
    CalcShifts --> ImagePairs["Generate pairs to\nperiodic images"]
    
    CenterPairs --> ZeroShift["shifts = (0,0,0)"]
    ImagePairs --> NonZeroShift["shifts = replica offsets"]
    
    ZeroShift --> Combine["Combine all pairs\nand shift indices"]
    NonZeroShift --> Combine
    
    Combine --> MapCoords["Map coordinates\nto central cell"]
    MapCoords --> NarrowDown["narrow_down:\nFilter by cutoff\nApply shifts"]
    
    NarrowDown --> Output["Neighbors with\nshift-corrected distances"]
    
    style CalcShifts fill:#f9f9f9
    style NarrowDown fill:#f9f9f9
```

**AllPairs PBC Algorithm**

The algorithm considers the central cell plus necessary periodic replicas, generating both within-cell pairs and cross-cell pairs with appropriate shift vectors.

**Sources:** [torchani/neighbors.py:189-214](), [torchani/neighbors.py:217-244]()

### Shift Vector Calculation

The `_all_pairs_pbc_shifts` function determines which periodic images must be considered:

[torchani/neighbors.py:252-277]()

The function:
- Computes the inverse cell (reciprocal lattice)
- Calculates how many cell replicas are needed in each direction based on cutoff
- Generates shift vectors for all required periodic images
- Excludes the central cell and symmetric images to avoid double counting

The shift vectors are integer triplets `(nx, ny, nz)` indicating multiples of cell vectors to add to coordinates when computing distances.

**Sources:** [torchani/neighbors.py:247-277]()

### CellList with PBC

The `CellList` algorithm also supports PBC. When PBC is enabled:

[torchani/neighbors.py:437-466]()

Key differences with PBC:
- Coordinates are **not** displaced (they remain in their input positions)
- The provided `cell` is used directly instead of computing a bounding cell
- Grid buckets can wrap around cell boundaries
- Shift indices track which periodic image each pair belongs to

The grid setup validates that the cell is large enough for the bucket size:

[torchani/neighbors.py:452-454]()

**Sources:** [torchani/neighbors.py:417-466](), [torchani/csrc/cell_list.cpp:282-316]()

## AEV Computation with PBC

### AEVComputer PBC Support

The `AEVComputer` class accepts `cell` and `pbc` parameters and passes them to the neighborlist:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Input["AEVComputer forward:\nspecies, coords, cell, pbc"]
    
    Input --> NL["Neighborlist:\nall_pairs or cell_list"]
    NL --> Neighbors["Neighbors object:\nindices, distances, diff_vectors"]
    
    Neighbors --> Radial["Radial AEV:\nCompute radial symmetry functions"]
    Neighbors --> Angular["Angular AEV:\nCompute angular symmetry functions"]
    
    Radial --> Concat["Concatenate\nRadial + Angular"]
    Angular --> Concat
    
    Concat --> AEV["AEV Tensor\n(molecules, atoms, aev_length)"]
    
    style NL fill:#f9f9f9
    style Radial fill:#f9f9f9
    style Angular fill:#f9f9f9
```

**AEV Computation with PBC**

The neighborlist handles all PBC complexity. Once neighbors are computed with correct shift-adjusted distances and difference vectors, the AEV computation proceeds identically to the non-PBC case.

**Sources:** [tests/test_aev.py:239-254](), [tests/test_aev.py:481-505]()

### Translational Invariance

A key property of AEVs with PBC is translational invariance: shifting all atoms by the same vector (including across cell boundaries) produces identical AEVs after wrapping:

[tests/test_aev.py:239-254]()

This test verifies that random translations produce identical AEVs, confirming correct PBC implementation.

**Sources:** [tests/test_aev.py:239-254]()

### Handling Cell Boundaries

Special care is taken for atoms at cell boundaries. The `TestAEVOnBoundary` test class verifies that atoms on corners, edges, and faces of the cell produce correct AEVs:

[tests/test_aev.py:335-388]()

The test places molecules at various positions (corners, edges, surfaces) relative to the cell, verifies they are correctly mapped to the central cell, and confirms AEVs are identical regardless of which image is used.

**Sources:** [tests/test_aev.py:335-388]()

## Key Classes and Functions

### Core PBC Functions

| Function | Location | Purpose |
|----------|----------|---------|
| `map_to_central` | [torchani/utils.py]() | Wrap coordinates into central unit cell |
| `_all_pairs_pbc` | [torchani/neighbors.py:217-244]() | Generate all pairs with PBC |
| `_all_pairs_pbc_shifts` | [torchani/neighbors.py:247-277]() | Calculate required shift vectors |
| `coords_to_fractional` | [torchani/neighbors.py:612-624]() | Convert Cartesian to fractional coordinates |
| `narrow_down` | [torchani/neighbors.py:66-115]() | Filter pairs by cutoff, apply shifts |

### Neighborlist Classes with PBC Support

| Class | Location | PBC Support |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| `AllPairs` | [torchani/neighbors.py:171-186]() | Full PBC support |
| `CellList` | [torchani/neighbors.py:300-317]() | Full PBC support |
| `FastCellList` | [torchani/neighbors.py:280-297]() | Full PBC support (C++ extension) |
| `AdaptiveList` | [torchani/neighbors.py:320-342]() | Full PBC support |
| `VerletCellList` | [torchani/neighbors.py:825-951]() | Full PBC support |

**Sources:** [torchani/neighbors.py:142-169](), [torchani/neighbors.py:171-343]()

## Usage Examples

### Basic PBC Calculation

```python
import torch
from torchani.aev import AEVComputer
from torchani.nn import SpeciesConverter

# Define cubic unit cell (10 Angstrom sides)
cell = torch.eye(3) * 10.0

# Enable PBC in all directions
pbc = torch.tensor([True, True, True])

# Atomic numbers and coordinates
species = torch.tensor([[1, 1, 8]])  # H, H, O
coords = torch.tensor([
    [[0.5, 0.5, 0.5],
     [9.8, 0.5, 0.5],  # Near boundary
     [5.0, 5.0, 5.0]]
])

# Convert to species indices
converter = SpeciesConverter(['H', 'C', 'N', 'O'])
species_idx = converter(species)

# Compute AEVs with PBC
aev_computer = AEVComputer.like_1x()
aevs = aev_computer(species_idx, coords, cell=cell, pbc=pbc)
```

**Sources:** [tests/test_aev.py:239-254]()

### Non-Orthogonal Cell

For non-orthogonal cells (e.g., monoclinic, triclinic):

```python
# Non-orthogonal cell
cell = torch.tensor([
    [10.0, 0.0, 0.0],   # a vector
    [0.0, 10.0, 0.0],   # b vector  
    [10.0, 0.0, 10.0]   # c vector (tilted)
])

pbc = torch.tensor([True, True, True])

# Atoms near boundary still interact correctly
coords = torch.tensor([[[0.1, 0.1, 0.05],
                         [10.0, 0.1, 0.1]]])
```

The cell list algorithm accounts for non-orthogonal cells via a spherical factor correction:

[torchani/neighbors.py:707-716]()

**Sources:** [tests/test_aev.py:316-332](), [torchani/neighbors.py:677-728]()

### Selective PBC

Enable PBC only in specific directions (e.g., slab geometry with PBC in xy-plane only):

```python
# PBC only in x and y directions (slab geometry)
pbc = torch.tensor([True, True, False])

cell = torch.eye(3) * 20.0

# Surface slab coordinates
coords = torch.tensor([[[...], [...], [...]]])
aevs = aev_computer(species_idx, coords, cell=cell, pbc=pbc)
```

Note: The current implementation requires PBC to be enabled in all directions or none. Selective PBC raises an error:

[torchani/csrc/cell_list.cpp:54-56]()

**Sources:** [torchani/csrc/cell_list.cpp:33-61]()

### Verifying PBC Correctness

Test that atoms at cell boundaries interact:

```python
import torch
from torchani.neighbors import AllPairs

cell = torch.eye(3) * 10.0
pbc = torch.tensor([True, True, True])
cutoff = 1.0

# Place atoms near opposite boundaries
species = torch.tensor([[0, 0]])
coords = torch.tensor([[[0.1, 0.1, 0.1],
                         [9.9, 0.0, 0.0]]])

# Should find neighbors due to PBC
neighborlist = AllPairs()
neighbors = neighborlist(cutoff, species, coords, cell, pbc)

# neighbors.indices should contain [0, 1] pair
print(neighbors.indices)  # [[0], [1]]
print(neighbors.distances)  # ~0.2 (wrapped distance)
```

**Sources:** [tests/test_aev.py:256-277]()

## Performance Considerations

### Computational Cost

PBC calculations are more expensive than non-PBC:

- `AllPairs`: Must consider multiple periodic images, increasing pair count
- `CellList`: Grid wrapping adds overhead, but remains O(N) scaling

The number of periodic images scales with `(cutoff / cell_size)³`. For small cells relative to cutoff, many images are needed.

### Cell Size Requirements

For `CellList` with PBC, the cell must be large enough to accommodate at least one bucket per dimension:

[torchani/neighbors.py:452-454]()

Minimum cell size ≈ cutoff × spherical_factor. For orthogonal cells, spherical_factor = 1. For highly non-orthogonal cells, it can be much larger.

**Sources:** [torchani/neighbors.py:437-466](), [torchani/neighbors.py:677-728]()

### Adaptive Selection

The `AdaptiveList` neighborlist automatically selects the optimal algorithm based on system size, including for PBC systems:

[torchani/neighbors.py:320-342]()

It uses different thresholds for PBC (`threshold=190`) vs non-PBC (`threshold_nopbc=1770`) cases.

**Sources:** [torchani/neighbors.py:320-342](), [torchani/neighbors.py:393-414]()

## Testing and Validation

TorchANI includes comprehensive PBC tests:

| Test Class | Purpose | Location |
|------------|---------|----------|
| `TestPBCSeeEachOther` | Verify atoms at boundaries interact | [tests/test_aev.py:234-333]() |
| `TestAEVOnBoundary` | Test AEVs at cell corners/edges/faces | [tests/test_aev.py:335-388]() |
| `TestAEVOnBenzenePBC` | Test repeated cells produce consistent AEVs | [tests/test_aev.py:390-437]() |
| `TestCellListComparison` | Verify CellList matches AllPairs with PBC | [tests/test_neighbors.py:173-261]() |

The tests verify:
- Translational invariance under cell wrapping
- Correct neighbor detection at boundaries
- Consistency between neighborlist algorithms
- Proper handling of non-orthogonal cells

**Sources:** [tests/test_aev.py:234-437](), [tests/test_neighbors.py:66-261]()

# Page: API Reference

# API Reference

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [examples/fundamentals.py](examples/fundamentals.py)
- [torchani/__init__.py](torchani/__init__.py)
- [torchani/models.py](torchani/models.py)
- [torchani/neurochem.py](torchani/neurochem.py)
- [torchani/utils.py](torchani/utils.py)

</details>



This page provides a comprehensive overview of the TorchANI public API. It documents all public classes, functions, and modules available for users building applications with TorchANI or training custom neural network potentials.

For practical usage examples and tutorials, see the [User Guide](#5). For detailed explanations of underlying concepts, see [Core Concepts](#4).

## Scope and Organization

The TorchANI API is organized into five major sections, each documented in detail in the following subsections:

- **[Core API](#9.1)**: Fundamental classes for computing energies, including `AEVComputer`, `ANINetworks`, `Ensemble`, `SpeciesConverter`, and gradient computation functions
- **[Model Factories](#9.2)**: Pre-trained model instantiation functions like `ANI1x()`, `ANI2x()`, `ANI1ccx()`, and `ANI2dr()`
- **[Datasets API](#9.3)**: Dataset loading, batching, and transformation utilities for training workflows
- **[ASE Calculator API](#9.4)**: Integration layer for using TorchANI models with the Atomic Simulation Environment
- **[Legacy NeuroChem API](#9.5)**: Backward-compatible interface for loading models in the original NeuroChem format

## Module Structure

TorchANI's API is organized into specialized modules, each handling a specific aspect of neural network potential computation:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "User Entry Points"
        models["torchani.models<br/>Pre-trained Models"]
        arch["torchani.arch<br/>Model Assembly"]
        grad["torchani.grad<br/>Energy & Forces"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Core Computation"
        aev["torchani.aev<br/>AEVComputer"]
        nn["torchani.nn<br/>ANINetworks, Ensemble<br/>SpeciesConverter"]
        neighbors["torchani.neighbors<br/>Neighborlist Algorithms"]
        potentials["torchani.potentials<br/>NNPotential, Repulsion, etc."]
    end
    
    subgraph "Training & Data"
        datasets["torchani.datasets<br/>Built-in Datasets"]
        transforms["torchani.transforms<br/>Data Preprocessing"]
        sae["torchani.sae<br/>Self-Energies"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Utilities"
        utils["torchani.utils<br/>Helper Functions"]
        units["torchani.units<br/>Unit Conversions"]
        constants["torchani.constants<br/>Physical Constants"]
        cutoffs["torchani.cutoffs<br/>Cutoff Functions"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Integration & Extensions"
        ase_calc["torchani.ase<br/>ASE Calculator"]
        neurochem["torchani.neurochem<br/>Legacy NeuroChem"]
        electro["torchani.electro<br/>Charge Prediction"]
    end
    
    models --> arch
    arch --> aev
    arch --> nn
    arch --> potentials
    aev --> neighbors
    datasets --> transforms
    grad --> nn
    ase_calc --> models
    neurochem --> models
```

**Sources**: [torchani/__init__.py:1-123]()

## Primary API Entry Points

Users typically interact with TorchANI through three main entry points:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Entry Point 1: Pre-built Models"
        factory["torchani.models.ANI2x()<br/>torchani.models.ANI1x()<br/>torchani.models.ANI1ccx()"]
        model["ANI Model Instance"]
        factory --> model
    end
    
    subgraph "Entry Point 2: Custom Assembly"
        assembler["torchani.arch.Assembler"]
        custom["Custom ANI Model"]
        assembler --> custom
    end
    
    subgraph "Entry Point 3: Direct Components"
        aev_comp["torchani.AEVComputer"]
        networks["torchani.ANINetworks"]
        converter["torchani.SpeciesConverter"]
        manual["Manual Pipeline"]
        aev_comp --> manual
        networks --> manual
        converter --> manual
    end
    
    model --> inference["Inference:<br/>model((species, coords))"]
    custom --> inference
    manual --> inference
```

**Sources**: [torchani/models.py:1-486](), [torchani/arch.py]() (referenced), [torchani/__init__.py:47-52]()

## Core Classes Overview

The following table summarizes the primary classes users interact with:

| Class | Module | Purpose | Documented In |
|-------|--------|---------|---------------|
| `ANI` | `torchani.arch` | Complete ANI model for energy prediction | [Core API](#9.1) |
| `ANIq` | `torchani.arch` | ANI model with charge prediction | [Core API](#9.1) |
| `AEVComputer` | `torchani.aev` | Computes atomic environment vectors | [Core API](#9.1) |
| `ANINetworks` | `torchani.nn` | Atomic neural networks for single element types | [Core API](#9.1) |
| `Ensemble` | `torchani.nn` | Container for ensemble of neural networks | [Core API](#9.1) |
| `SpeciesConverter` | `torchani.nn` | Converts atomic numbers to element indices | [Core API](#9.1) |
| `SelfEnergy` | `torchani.sae` | Self-atomic energy calculator | [Core API](#9.1) |
| `Assembler` | `torchani.arch` | Builder for constructing custom models | [Core API](#9.1) |
| `ANIDataset` | `torchani.datasets` | Dataset loader for HDF5/Parquet/Zarr | [Datasets API](#9.3) |
| `Batcher` | `torchani.datasets` | Splits data into train/validation batches | [Datasets API](#9.3) |
| `Calculator` | `torchani.ase` | ASE calculator interface | [ASE Calculator API](#9.4) |

**Sources**: [torchani/__init__.py:47-52](), [torchani/models.py:1-62]()

## API Conventions

### Input Format

All TorchANI models and computational components expect inputs in a consistent format:

```mermaid
graph LR
    input["Input Tuple<br/>(species, coordinates)"]
    species["species: Tensor<br/>shape: (molecules, atoms)<br/>dtype: torch.long<br/>values: atomic numbers"]
    coords["coordinates: Tensor<br/>shape: (molecules, atoms, 3)<br/>dtype: torch.float32/64<br/>units: Angstroms"]
    optional["Optional:<br/>cell, pbc"]
    
    input --> species
    input --> coords
    input -.-> optional
```

**Sources**: [examples/fundamentals.py:33-44](), [torchani/models.py:25-30]()

### Output Format

Model outputs are returned as structured tuples with named fields:

| Method | Return Type | Fields | Units |
|--------|-------------|--------|-------|
| `model((species, coords))` | `SpeciesEnergies` | `species`, `energies` | Hartrees |
| `model.atomic_energies(...)` | `SpeciesAtomicEnergies` | `species`, `energies` | Hartrees |
| `model.energies_qbcs(...)` | `SpeciesEnergiesQBCs` | `species`, `energies`, `qbcs` | Hartrees (energies) |
| `energies_and_forces(...)` | `tuple` | `(energies, forces)` | Hartrees, Hartree/Å |

**Sources**: [torchani/models.py:40-58]()

### Device and Dtype Management

All components support explicit device and dtype specification:

```python
# Example API pattern (not executable)
model = torchani.models.ANI2x(device='cuda', dtype=torch.float32)
aev_computer = torchani.AEVComputer(..., device='cpu', dtype=torch.float64)
```

**Sources**: [torchani/models.py:86-89](), [examples/fundamentals.py:61-67]()

## Namespace Organization

TorchANI provides convenient access to frequently-used classes directly from the top-level namespace:

```mermaid
graph TB
    torchani["import torchani"]
    
    torchani --> conv["torchani.SpeciesConverter"]
    torchani --> aev["torchani.AEVComputer"]
    torchani --> net["torchani.ANINetworks"]
    torchani --> ens["torchani.Ensemble"]
    torchani --> sae["torchani.SelfEnergy"]
    torchani --> sp["torchani.single_point()"]
    
    torchani --> modules["Submodules:<br/>models, datasets, nn,<br/>aev, neighbors, etc."]
    
    note["Also available from<br/>original modules:<br/>torchani.nn.SpeciesConverter<br/>torchani.aev.AEVComputer<br/>etc."]
    
    conv -.-> note
    aev -.-> note
```

**Sources**: [torchani/__init__.py:47-94]()

```python
import torchani
print(torchani.__version__)
```

The version is obtained from package metadata at runtime.

## Common Utilities

The `torchani.utils` module provides helper classes and functions used throughout the API:

| Utility | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `ChemicalSymbolsToInts` | Convert element symbols to integer indices |
| `IntsToChemicalSymbols` | Convert integer indices to element symbols |
| `AtomicNumbersToChemicalSymbols` | Convert atomic numbers to element symbols |
| `ChemicalSymbolsToAtomicNumbers` | Convert element symbols to atomic numbers |
| `AtomicNumbersToMasses` | Convert atomic numbers to atomic masses |
| `pad_atomic_properties()` | Pad molecular properties to uniform size |
| `strip_redundant_padding()` | Remove excess padding from tensors |

**Sources**: [torchani/utils.py:23-40](), [torchani/utils.py:285-468]()

## Constants and Physical Data

Standard physical constants and atomic data are available in dedicated modules:

- **`torchani.constants`**: Physical constants and periodic table data
- **`torchani.units`**: Unit conversion utilities (Hartree, eV, kcal/mol, etc.)
- **`torchani.utils.PERIODIC_TABLE`**: Element symbols indexed by atomic number
- **`torchani.utils.ATOMIC_NUMBER`**: Atomic numbers indexed by symbol
- **`torchani.utils.MASS`**: Atomic masses

Predefined element sets for specific models:

- **`torchani.utils.SYMBOLS_1X`**: `("H", "C", "N", "O")` - ANI-1x/ANI-1ccx models
- **`torchani.utils.SYMBOLS_2X`**: `("H", "C", "N", "O", "S", "F", "Cl")` - ANI-2x models

**Sources**: [torchani/utils.py:19-65](), [torchani/__init__.py:19-41]()
